parole.significato: used with a stem to form the first-person plural past historic of regular -are verbs
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *-āvmus, from Latin -āvimus.

parole.significato: used with an infinitive stem to form the conditional mood.
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin hĕbui / (h)ĕ(bu)i, which stems from classical Latin habuī, first-person singular perfect of habeō. See -erei.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the first-person plural past historic of regular -ere verbs
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *hebuimus, which stems from classical Latin habuimus, first-person plural perfect of habeō. See -eremmo.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the third-person singular conditional of regular -are and -ere verbs
parole.testo: From -er- + -ebbe. * -er- is the reduced form of the Italian infinitive endings -are and -ere. * -ebbe stems from Vulgar Latin hĕbuit, which stems from classical Latin habuit, third-person singular perfect of habeō. See -erei.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the third-person plural conditional of regular -are and -ere verbs
parole.testo: From -er- + -ebbero. * -er- is the reduced form of the Italian infinitive endings -are and -ere. * -ebbero stems from Vulgar Latin hĕbuerunt, which stems from classical Latin habuērunt, third-person plural perfect of habeō. See Italian -erei.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the first-person singular conditional of regular -are and -ere verbs
parole.testo: From -er- + -ei. * -er- is the reduced form of the Italian infinitive endings -are and -ere. * -ei stems from Vulgar Latin hĕbui / (h)ĕ(bu)i, from classical Latin habuī, first-person singular perfect of habeō. The Italian conditional mood stems from a Vulgar Latin periphrastic verb form consisting o

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the first-person plural conditional of regular -are and -ere verbs
parole.testo: From -er- + -emmo. * -er- is the reduced form of the Italian infinitive endings -are and -ere. * -emmo stems from Vulgar Latin hĕbuimus, which stems from classical Latin habuimus, first-person plural perfect of habeō. See -erei.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the second-person plural conditional of regular -are and -ere verbs
parole.testo: From -er- + -este. * -er- is the reduced form of the Italian infinitive endings -are and -ere. * -este stems from Vulgar Latin hĕbuistis, which stems from classical Latin habuistis, second-person plural perfect of habeō. See Italian -erei.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the second-person singular conditional of regular -are and -ere verbs
parole.testo: From -er- + -esti. * -er- is the reduced form of the Italian infinitive endings -are and -ere. * -esti stems from Vulgar Latin hĕbuisti, which stems from classical Latin habuistī, second-person singular perfect of habeō. See Italian -erei.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the first-person singular future of regular -are verbs
parole.testo: A combination of the verb suffix -are (where the a was reduced to e) or -ere with ho, first person singular present indicative of avere. This traces back to a Vulgar Latin periphrastic construction of forming the future using the infinitive of the verb + habeō, e.g. parlerò, from Vulgar Latin *parab

parole.significato: forms adjectives (sometimes used as nouns) that indicate relationship, membership, quality
parole.testo: From Late Latin, Vulgar Latin -iscus. Cognates: see Proto-Germanic *-iskaz.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the second-person plural past historic and imperfect subjunctive of regular -ere verbs
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin hĕbuistis, which stems from classical Latin habuistis, second-person plural perfect of habeō. See -ereste.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the second-person singular past historic of regular -ere verbs
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin hĕbuisti, which stems from classical Latin habuistī, second-person singular perfect of habeō. See -eresti.

parole.significato: forms nouns and adjectives indicating geographical origin
parole.testo: Uncertain. Or * from a Vulgar Latin development of Latin ē(n)s(is) + -iānum. Compare Italian -ese, -iano, both relation-forming suffixes. * from a Vulgar Latin development of Latin -it- + -iānum. Compare Italian artigiano, cortigiano, partigiano.

parole.significato: used to derive adjectives and nouns indicating a state or condition
parole.testo: Via Vulgar Latin *-ingus, from Proto-West Germanic *-ing, from Proto-Germanic *-ingaz (“belonging to; coming from”).

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the first-person singular future of regular -ire verbs
parole.testo: A combination of the verb suffix -ire with ho, first person singular present indicative of avere. This traces back to a Vulgar Latin periphrastic construction of forming the future using the infinitive of the verb + habeō, e.g. seguirò, from Vulgar Latin *sequīre habeō.

parole.significato: suffix used to form diminutives, especially with an endearing connotation
parole.testo: Perhaps a variant of -etto, or from Vulgar Latin *-ottum.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the third-person singular past historic of regular -are verbs
parole.testo: As the third person singular first conjugation past historic ending, from earlier -ao, from Vulgar Latin *-aut, from Classical Latin -āvit. Example: Italian lodò, from Latin laudavit. As the first person singular future indicative ending, from ho, first person singular of avere. Ho was contracted fr
Corresponds to a Vulgar Latin *ad retrō.

parole.significato: to beat down with a pole (fruit from a tree)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *abbaclāre, from ab- (“off, away”) + baculum (“stick”). By surface analysis, a- + bacchio (“rod, stick”) + -are (1st conjugation suffix).
From Vulgar Latin *abbiberāre, derived ultimately from Classical Latin bibere (“drink”).
From a- + braccio (“arm”) + -are, possibly corresponding to a Vulgar Latin *adbracchiāre, from Latin ad- + bracchium + -o. Compare Spanish abrazar.

parole.significato: fir, fir tree, particularly the silver fir (Abies alba)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *abētem, from Classical Latin abietem.

parole.significato: to abhor, to detest, to loathe
parole.testo: Latinization of older abborrire, inherited from Vulgar Latin *abhorrīre, itself from Latin abhorrēre, derived from ab- (“from, away from”) + horreō (“tremble; dread”).

parole.significato: The name of the Latin script letter H/h.; aitch
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *acca (“aitch”).
From Vulgar Latin *adquassiāre, derived from Latin quassus, perfect passive participle of quatiō (“to shake, agitate”).
From a merger of Vulgar Latin *accaptāre (“to take, accept”), *accattāre (“to watch, heed”) and *accapitāre (“to grab, catch”).

parole.significato: to catch, to grab, to seize
parole.testo: From a- + chiappare, from Vulgar Latin *clapāre, from Late Latin capulāre. Cognate with Sicilian acchiappari.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *acia, from Latin acies (“sharp edge”).
From Vulgar Latin *accolligere, derived from Classical Latin ad- + colligere (whence the Italian cogliere).

parole.significato: to shorten; to abridge; to abbreviate
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *adcurtiāre, from Latin curtus. Compare Sicilian accurzari.

parole.significato: to conciliate, to bring to agreement
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *accordāre, derived from Latin cor (“heart”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *accorrigere, from Latin ad- + corrigō (“to correct”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *aquiducium, derived from Late Latin aquiductus, itself the alternative form of Classical aquaeductus.
From Vulgar Latin *acquīsītāre, from Latin acquīsītus, ultimately from Latin adquīrere.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *aquatrinum.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *addīrēctiāre, from *dīrēctiāre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *addessum. Documented since the late thirteenth century.
From Vulgar Latin *adoculāre, from oclus, from Latin oculus. Compare Portuguese olhar.
From older dunche, inherited from Vulgar Latin *dunquam.
From Vulgar Latin *adūsāre, derived from Classical Latin ūsus, perfect participle of ūtor (“to use, to employ”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *adferrāre, from ferrum (“iron, sword”).

parole.significato: to drown (to kill by suffocating in a liquid)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *affōcāre, alteration of Latin offōcāre.

parole.significato: to sink (to submerge into a liquid; to cause to be submerged into a liquid)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *affundāre, from Latin ad + fundus (“bottom”). By surface analysis, a- + fondo + -are.

parole.significato: to hasten, hurry up, speed up, quicken, rush
parole.testo: From a- + fretta + -are, presumed from Vulgar Latin frictare, from frictus, past participle of fricare.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *affrontāre, from Latin ad- + frons + -āre. By surface analysis, a- + fronte + -are.
From Vulgar Latin *affūmāre, ultimately from Latin fūmus (“smoke”, noun). By surface analysis, a- + fumo + -are.

parole.significato: to yearn, to long for, to crave
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *agōniāre, from Ancient Greek ἀγωνιάω (agōniáō, “I struggle”).
From Vulgar Latin agustus, from Latin augustus. Doublet of Augusto.

Ultimately derived from Vulgar Latin ācrus, from Classical Latin ācrem (with a change in declension). Likely borrowed from Gallo-Italic, mostly displacing the inherited and now rare acro. Cognate with Sicilian agru. Doublet of acre, a borrowing from Latin.
From Vulgar Latin or Medieval Latin ācrūmen (“something sour or bitter”), ultimately from Latin ācer (“sharp, sour, bitter”). Cognate to Old French aigrun (“sour fruit”).
From earlier *acuzzare, from Vulgar Latin *acūtiāre, a verb based on Latin acūtus (“sharp”). Cognate with French aiguiser, Catalan and Occitan agusar, Portuguese aguçar, Spanish aguzar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *alba, from Latin albus (“white”). Compare French aube.
Derived, with the diminutive suffix -ello, from a Vulgar Latin *albaster, *albastrum (whence also Romanian albastru (“blue”)), from Latin albus (“white”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *albizāre. Derivable from alba (“dawn”, noun) + -eggiare (verb-forming suffix) and, for sense 2, albo (“white”) + -eggiare.
Possibly from a Vulgar Latin *albarus, a derivative of Latin albus (“white”).
From Vulgar Latin *alicūnus, from Classical Latin aliquem (“someone, something”) + ūnum (“one”). Cognate with French aucun, Spanish alguno, Galician algún, Portuguese algum.

parole.significato: to turn pale (through shock or fright)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *adlīvēre / *adlīvēscere, derived from Latin līvēre.
From Vulgar Latin *allevus, from allevo. Compare Sicilian aḍḍevu.
From a Vulgar Latin *alaudula, the diminutive of Latin alauda (“lark”), of Gaulish origin. Doublet of alauda.

parole.significato: another person's, someone else's, other people's, of others
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *alterūi, corresponding to Classical Latin alterī (dative singular of alter). The -ui ending, analogous to lui, colui, costui, cotestui, codestui, is ultimately due to the influence of Latin cui. Compare French autrui.
From Vulgar Latin *helciaria, from Latin helcium (“collar harness”).

parole.significato: to lift (up), to raise, to heave
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *altiāre, derived from Latin altus (“high”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *amblāre, syncopated form of Latin ambulāre. Doublet of ambulare. Cf. also andare.
Uncertain, perhaps from Vulgar Latin *invāgīnāre, from vāgīna.
Possibly from Vulgar Latin *admicāre or from a- + micāre.
From Vulgar Latin *admortīre, derived from Latin mortuus (“dead”). By surface analysis, a- + morto + -ire.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *admortiāre, probably from *admortīre, from Latin ad + mortem.
From Vulgar Latin *amōrōsus, derived from Latin amōrem (“love”). By surface analysis, amore + -oso.
From Vulgar Latin *anatria, from Latin anatem, from Proto-Italic *anats, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂énh₂t- (“duck”).
From Vulgar Latin *hanca, from Proto-Germanic *hankō, related to *ankijǭ (“joint, limb”). Compare French hanche, English haunch.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *hancōra, probably from Late Latin in hanc hōram (“until this hour”). Compare French encore, Occitan and Catalan encara.

parole.significato: to water (plants or streets) by sprinkling water
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *inafflāre, from in- + afflāre, from ad- + flāre (“to blow”).
From anno + -ata, or perhaps from a Vulgar Latin *annāta, from Latin annāre; compare French année.

parole.significato: to drown, to kill by drowning
parole.testo: From earlier *annecare, from Vulgar Latin *adnecāre (“to drown”), derived from Latin necō (“to kill”). Compare Sicilian annigari, Spanish anegar, Romanian îneca, French noyer.
Ultimately from Vulgar Latin *anteānus. Documented from the thirteenth century.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *appariculāre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ad poenam. By surface analysis, univerbation of a + pena (“pain, trouble”). Compare French à peine, Spanish apenas, etc.

parole.significato: synonym of accendere (“turn on, play, light up”)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *appiciāre, from ad + pix (“pitch, tar”). Alternatively of onomatopoeic origin.

parole.significato: (typically with a or su) to glue (to)
parole.testo: From Tuscan appicciare, from Vulgar Latin *appiciāre, from ad + pix, pĭcis (“pitch, tar”). Alternatively of onomatopoeic origin.

parole.significato: to support, to second, to back, to endorse
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *appodiāre, from Latin podium. Compare French appuyer, Spanish apoyar and Portuguese apoiar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *arbuscellum, a diminutive ultimately based on Latin arbor (“tree”).
From Vulgar Latin *arciōnem, from Latin arcus (“bow”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ārdĕre, from Latin ārdēre.
From Vulgar Latin argerem, from Latin aggerem (“rubble; mound; rampart”).
Probably from a Vulgar Latin *harpigōnem, from Latin harpagōnem, from Ancient Greek ἁρπάγη (harpágē). Doublet of arpagone and arpone.

parole.significato: to halt, to stop, to check, to staunch
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *arrestāre, from Latin ad- (“to”) + restō, restāre (“stop, remain behind, stay back”).

From Latin arte (“by skill”, ablative of ars (“art”)) + Latin factum (“thing made”, from facio (“to make, do"”)). Equivalent to a possible Proto-Romance or Vulgar Latin *artefactum (compare Portuguese artefato, Spanish artefacto); see also artifex (“artist”).

From earlier *articiano, from Vulgar Latin *artitiānus, from Latin artītus (“skilled”), past participle of artīre (“to instruct in arts”), from ars (“art, skill”). Cognate with Sicilian articianu, Venetan artexan, Friulian artesan and Piedmontese artisan.

parole.significato: each of the two pieces of wood flanking the shaft of the harrow
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *axālis. Doublet of assale and sala.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *haspa. Doublet of aspo.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *haspa. Doublet of aspa.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *axālis. Doublet of asciale and sala.

parole.significato: to put in order, to organize, to tidy up (a room, etc.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *asseditāre, from ad- + sedeō (“to sit”) + -itō (forms frequentative verbs).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *assēcūrāre. By surface analysis, a- + sicuro + -are.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *axīlis.
Probably from a Vulgar Latin *assus, from Classical Latin as.
From Vulgar Latin *(as)similiāre, a verb based on Latin similis (“similar”). By surface analysis, a- + somigliare. Doublet of assimilare and assembrare.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *attīnctus as the perfect passive participle of Latin attingō instead of attāctus. Compare French atteint.
From the past participle of attortigliare, from Vulgar Latin *tortiliāre, from Latin tortilis (“twisted, coiled”).

parole.significato: to cause a sweet smell, to waft perfume
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin *aulēre, diphthongized form of Latin olēre (with a later change in a conjugation), from an earlier form olō, from Proto-Italic *odō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ed- (“to smell”). Doublet of olire.

parole.significato: to make accustomed, to get used, to accustom, to habituate
parole.testo: Derived — perhaps through the influence of Old French auser or Old Occitan ausar — from Vulgar Latin *adūsāre, derived from ad- (“to, towards”) + ūsus (“use; practice; experience; habit”) + -ō (1ˢᵗ-conjugation verbal suffix). Doublet of adusare.

parole.significato: to advance, to proceed (to move forward)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *abanteāre, from Late Latin ab ante, from ab + ante.
From Vulgar Latin *adventūra.

From a Vulgar Latin *advitiāre, from *vitiāre (“accustom, habituate”), from Latin vitium. Compare Spanish avezar, vezar, Portuguese vezar, avezar, Occitan avezar, envezar, Catalan avesar, and cf. also Romanian învăța.
From Vulgar Latin *advinculāre, from Late Latin vinculāre, from vinculum.
From Vulgar Latin *bábbọ, accusative-ablative form of *bábbọs, childish term of onomatopoeic origin.
From Vulgar Latin *baccalārem (see: baccalārius).
From Vulgar Latin *baclitta, a diminutive from Latin baculum.
From a Vulgar Latin *opacīvus, from Latin opācus (“shady”). Cf. also dialectal ombaco.
From Vulgar Latin *baneāre, from Late Latin balneāre, from Latin balneum. Compare French baigner, Sicilian vagnari, Spanish bañar.
From Vulgar Latin *barbūtus (“bearded”). By surface analysis, barba (“beard”) + -uto.

Vulgar Latin *barilus or *barillus, perhaps via Old French baril, as a direct inheritance would yield *barilo. Stated by Vocabolario etimologico della lingua italiana to be of Celtic origin, however a more likely origin is Proto-West Germanic *baril, from Proto-Germanic *barilaz, cf. the etymology f
From Vulgar Latin *barra, possibly from Gaulish *barros (“the bushy end”). Doublet of bar.
From Vulgar Latin *barrica, from *barra, possibly ultimately from Gaulish.

parole.significato: to feel faint, to faint, to swoon (of hunger, heat, cold, etc.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *basīre, maybe of Celtic origin.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bastāre (“to be enough; to suffice”), possibly derived from a modification of Late Latin bastum (“stick, staff, rod, pole”), from Ancient Greek βαστάζω (bastázō, “to lift, carry, bear, support (weight)”). Compare Sicilian bastari, Spanish and Portuguese bastar, French ba
From Vulgar Latin *bastīre (“to build; sew”).
From Vulgar Latin *bat(t)uāculum, from Latin bat(t)uere (“beat”). Synonym and doublet of battaglio, which was borrowed via Occitan.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *baba, of infantile/nursery origin.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bene venūtus, presumably a calque of a Frankish term, derived from Proto-Germanic *wiljakwemô (“a welcome guest or arrival”), from which many modern Germanic forms descend, such as English welcome. By surface analysis, ben (“well”, apocopic form of bene) + venuto (“come”
From Vulgar Latin *bibanda, from Latin bibenda, from bibendum.
Perhaps from Vulgar Latin *blaesāre, derived from Latin blaesus (“lisping, stammering”, adjective).
Perhaps from a Vulgar Latin root *oblaecus, from Classical Latin oblīquus.

parole.significato: to divide something into two branches; to bifurcate
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *bifurcāre, from Latin bifurcātus.

Probably from Vulgar Latin *bysseus, from Latin byssus (“linen”), whence bisso; cognate with English and French beige; French bis; Ligurian and Venetan bixo. However, compare badius (“brownish color”). Doublet of Bixio (a surname).

parole.significato: wooden bucket wider and lower than the bigoncia, unflared and with two holes through which a stave is inserted for carr…
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bicongius, from bi- (“twice”) + congius (“unit of liquid measure”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bilancia, from Latin bilanx (“balance with two scalepans”), from bi- (see Latin bis) and lanx.
Deverbal from bilicare (“to balance”) + -o, itself inherited from Vulgar Latin *umbilicāre, derived from Latin umbilicus.
Probably from Vulgar Latin *budula, diminutive of Late Latin buda.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bisonium, borrowed from Frankish *bisunnija.

From Vulgar Latin, Late Latin bovārius or boārius (“cow herder”), from Latin bovārius or boārius (“of cattle”), from bōs (“ox”). By surface analysis, bove + -aro. Compare French bouvier, Portuguese boieiro, Romanian boar, Spanish boyero. Doublet of boario.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *buttia, borrowed from Byzantine Greek βούττια (boúttia, plural of βούττιον (boúttion)), from Ancient Greek βοῦττις (boûttis), possibly borrowed from Pre-Greek. See also bozza.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bonacia.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin, of pre-Indo-European origin.
From Vulgar Latin *brandus, of Germanic origin.
Diminutive of (rare) bricia (“crumb, etc.”), palatalized form of brisa, from Vulgar Latin *brisāre (“to break”). Cf. sbrisolona.
From Vulgar Latin *brūsicāre, *brūsiāre; compare bruciare (“to burn”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *upupula, from Latin upupa.
From Vulgar Latin *būcāta, from Frankish *būkōn (“to submerge; to wash”). Cognate with Catalan bugada and French buée.
From Vulgar Latin *boem, from Latin bovem (“cow, bull, or ox”). Compare Spanish buey. Doublet of bove.
From Vulgar Latin *bullicāre, a frequentative based on Latin bullīre.

Probably from Vulgar Latin *burrula, diminutive of Late Latin burra (“nonsense, trickery”, literally “flock of wool”), possibly through the intermediate of Spanish burla (unless itself comes instead from Italian).

parole.significato: belly of an animal (especially of birds)
parole.testo: Uncertain. Likely from Vulgar Latin *būceum (“hollow inside”), from Vulgar Latin *būca (“cavity”). Compare buzzico.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cacca, possibly cognate if not directly from Ancient Greek κάκκη (kákkē, “dung”). Compare Romagnol càca, Sicilian cacca.
From Vulgar Latin *caclus, *catlus, contraction of Latin catulus (“young puppy or kitten”).

parole.significato: to hunt, to prey on (of animals)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *captiāre, from Latin captus. Doublet of cazzare.

Cf. Old Italian caduno, catuno, from Vulgar Latin *catūnum, from Latin cata (< Ancient Greek κατά (katá)) + unum. The form cadauno may be through the intermediate of Old Spanish cada uno. Compare Occitan cadun, Catalan cadascun; cf. French chacun. See also ciascuno.
From Vulgar Latin *cadentia, from Latin cadēns, present participle of cadō (“to fall”). Doublet of chance.
From Vulgar Latin *cadūtus, past participle for Late Latin cadēre, from Latin cadĕre.

From cagione + -are or less likely from a Vulgar Latin *occāsionāre, from Latin occāsiāre. Cf. also accagionare, possibly from a root *accāsionāre. Compare Old French achoisoner, Romanian cășuna, cf. also Spanish ocasionar.

From Vulgar Latin *coāglāre, *quāglāre, from syncopation of Latin coāgulāre. Compare French cailler, Portuguese coalhar, Spanish cuajar, Sicilian cuagghiari, Sardinian cazare or cracare. See also the borrowed doublet coagulare.
From Vulgar Latin, Late Latin quāglum/ *coāglum, from Latin coāgulum. Doublet of coagulo, a borrowing.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cania.
Via a Vulgar Latin *calāre, possibly ultimately from a pre-Roman language. Related are French cale and Spanish cala.
Possibly from a Vulgar Latin form *carabriōnem, from Latin crābrōnem, from Proto-Italic *krāzrō, from a Proto-Indo-European form *krH-s-r-o, from the root *ḱerh₂- (“head”).
From Vulgar Latin *calcīna, from Latin calcem.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *calidizāre. Derivable from caldo + -eggiare.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin cambiāre, from change in conjugation of cambīre. Doublet of cangiare. Cognate with Neapolitan cagnà.
From Vulgar Latin *camellus, from Latin camēlus, from Ancient Greek κάμηλος (kámēlos), of Semitic origin.

parole.significato: to walk, to tread, to travel, to wander, to stroll, to saunter
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cammīnāre. By surface analysis, cammino + -are. Compare French cheminer, Spanish caminar and Portuguese caminhar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *canālia, from canis, corresponding to cane + -aglia.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *canīle; compare French chenil. By surface analysis, cane + -ile.

From Vulgar Latin *canthus (“corner”), from Gaulish *cantos, denoting the location for liquor storage, from Proto-Celtic *cantos (“corner”), from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂ndʰ-. Perhaps cognate with Ancient Greek κανθός (kanthós, “corner of the eye”), but this is unconvincing.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *capillūtus. By surface analysis, capello + -uto.

parole.significato: headland (strip of uncultivated land, at the edge of a field, where the plough turns)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *capitianea, from Latin capitium. See also cavedagna, a northern variant.
From Vulgar Latin *capitiale, from Latin capitium. Compare Spanish cabezal, Portuguese cabeçal, Old French chevecier, Catalan capçal, Occitan cabeçal.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *capitāre, from Latin caput. Compare Romanian căpăta.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin capus, from Latin caput, from Proto-Italic *kaput, from Proto-Indo-European *káput. Doublet of chef.
From Vulgar Latin *caplus, contracted form of Latin capulus. Compare Sicilian ncacchiu.
From Vulgar Latin *cappō, *cappōnem, from Latin cāpō. Compare English capon, French chapon, Portuguese capão, Spanish capón.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *carōnia, from Latin carō (“flesh, meat”). Compare French charogne.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cāsicāre, derived from Latin cadere. Compare Sicilian cascari.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *casora, from Latin casa. Cf. Romanian căsuri, Aromanian cãsuri.

parole.significato: catafalque (platform used to display or convey a coffin)
parole.testo: Perhaps from Vulgar Latin *catafalicum, derived from Ancient Greek κατά (katá, “down”) + Latin fala (“scaffolding, wooden siege tower”). Also influenced scaffold.
From Vulgar Latin *cavaneus, ultimately from Latin cavus (“hollow”). Cognate with Sicilian cavagnu.
From Vulgar Latin capitia, from the neuter plural of capitium (reanalyzed as a feminine singular), from caput.
Uncertain: possibly from Vulgar Latin *centium, from Latin centō, from Ancient Greek κέντρων (kéntrōn).
From Vulgar Latin *citriŏlum. Doublet of citrullo.
From Vulgar Latin *clapāre, metathesis of *caplāre, contraction of Late Latin capulāre, from Latin capulum (“handle, hilt”). Compare Venetan ciapar, Friulian cjapâ, Lombard ciapà.

Probably from Vulgar Latin *classum, formed to Latin classicum (“trumpet signal to the troops”) and Late Latin conclassō (“to muster”), originally nautical terms. As such, related but not derived from the word under Etymology 2.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *clavĭca, from Late Latin clavăca, clovăca, for Latin cloāca. Doublet of cloaca, a borrowing.

From a hypothetical Vulgar Latin *clociola, diminutive of *clocea, from metathesis of Latin cochlea (“snail”), borrowed from Ancient Greek κοχλίας (kokhlías), cognate with κόχλος (kókhlos, “shellfish”). Compare with Sardinian còciola and Sicilian còzzula.
From Vulgar Latin *cloma, through metathesis and syncopation of Latin comula (“pretty hair”), diminutive of coma (“hair of the head”).
From Vulgar Latin quī sapit (“who knows”). Cognate with Spanish and Galician quizá, Portuguese quiçá. By surface analysis, univerbation of chi + sa, literally “who knows”.
From Vulgar Latin *cisque-unus, from Latin quisque ūnus, and influenced by cadauno. Cf. French chacun, Catalan cadascun.
From a Vulgar Latin *caelestrum, from a change in declension of Medieval Latin caelestris, from a substitution in suffix of Classical Latin caelestis, derived from caelum (“sky; heaven”).
From Vulgar Latin *incīsculāre, derived from Classical Latin incīsus, perfect passive participle of incīdō (“to cut open”).
From Vulgar Latin *cingla, syncopated form of Late Latin cingula, from the plural of Latin cingulum.

From an earlier *singhiale, *singhiare, from Vulgar Latin *singlāris, from syncopation of Latin singulāris [porcus]. Compare Catalan senglar, Occitan singlar, French sanglier, Friulian cenglâr. Doublet of singolare.
From Vulgar Latin *cinglum, from Latin cingulum. Doublet of cingolo.
From Vulgar Latin *tsucca, borrowed from Gaulish *tsukka, from Proto-Celtic *tsŭkk-, from Proto-Germanic *stukkaz (“stock; stump”). Compare Sicilian zuccu.
Perhaps inherited from Vulgar Latin *extruncāre.
From Vulgar Latin *exundulāre, from unda (“wave”).

Probably from a Vulgar Latin *cytula where ⟨y⟩ was i̯u or also *cyatula after cyathus (“small ladle”) altered from Latin cotyla (“a kind of cup without handles”), from Ancient Greek κοτύλη (kotúlē, “cup, beaker”).

Possibly a reduced form of earlier *piccitto, probably from Vulgar Latin pittitus (“small, worthless”). Related to piccolo and piccino (“little, small”), and a doublet of zito. Compare Piedmontese cit (“small; boy, kid”), Ligurian citto (“cent; centimeter”). By the way, compare also English chit, fo

parole.significato: this, that (referring to an object close to the addressee)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Italian cotesto, from Old Italian cotevesto, contracted from a Vulgar Latin introductory locution *eccum tibi istum; compare *eccum iste whence Italian questo.
From Vulgar Latin *cōlea n pl, from Latin cōleus m sg.
From Vulgar Latin *colātīcius, from Latin colāre. By surface analysis, colato + -iccio.
Contracted from Vulgar Latin *eccum illaei, (genitive-)dative feminine singular of *eccum ille, under the influence of *illui. Cognate to Italian lei.
From Vulgar Latin colla, from Ancient Greek κόλλα (kólla, “glue”). Compare French colle, Sicilian coḍḍa, Spanish and Portuguese cola.
From Vulgar Latin *eccum illorum, genitive(-dative) plural of *eccum ille, also the source of quello. Compare Romanian acelor and Old French celeur.
Contracted from Vulgar Latin *eccum illui, (genitive-)dative masculine singular of *eccum ille, under the influence of Latin cui (“to whom”). Compare French celui. and Romanian acelui.
From Vulgar Latin *eccum illāc, from Latin eccum + illāc.
From Vulgar Latin *combattere, from Latin cum + battuō.
From Vulgar Latin *culmineum, from Latin culmen.

parole.significato: to begin, to start, to commence, to set about
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cominitiāre.
Derived from older compagna (assimilated to -ia), from Vulgar Latin *compānia. By surface analysis, compagna (“companion”) + -ia (abstract noun-forming suffix).

parole.significato: to have pity for; to feel sorry for
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *compatīre, from Latin compatī.

parole.significato: to spell or spell out by slowly pronouncing
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *compitāre, modified from Latin computāre (“count, reckon”). Doublet of contare and computare, respectively inherited and borrowed from Latin.
From Vulgar Latin *compitus, from Latin computus. Doublet of computo and conto.
From Vulgar Latin *comperāre, from Latin comparāre (“to prepare, procure, get, purchase, obtain”), from cum + parō. Compare Portuguese and Spanish comprar, Romanian cumpăra.
From Vulgar Latin *comptiāre, from Latin comptus. Compare Sicilian cunzari, Venetan consar, conzsar, Catalan acunçar.

parole.significato: to sugarcoat, to coat with sugar
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *cōnfectāre, frequentative of Latin cōnficiō, through its past participle cōnfectus. Compare Spanish cohechar, Portuguese confeitar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *conquista (“conquest”). Compare Spanish conquista, French conquête. By surface analysis, conquistare (“to conquer”) + -a.
Probably from a Vulgar Latin *conquisitāre, derived from Latin conquisitus, perfect passive participle of conquirō. Cf. also conquista. Compare Occitan, Catalan, Portuguese, and Spanish conquistar.

parole.significato: to achieve, to attain, to get, to gain
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *cōnsequīre, or *cōnsequere, remodeled after Latin cōnsequī. Compare Spanish and Portuguese conseguir.
From Vulgar Latin *contu(s), *comptu(s), from Latin computus. Doublet of computo and compito.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *contrāta. Compare French contrée.

parole.significato: to invite to a dinner etc.
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *convītāre, from Latin invītāre (“to invite”).
From Vulgar Latin *coperclum, from Latin cooperculum, from cooperiō.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cōpla, from Latin cōpula. Doublet of copula, which was borrowed. Compare Sicilian cucchia.

parole.significato: leather (especially when stamped with a design)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *coriāmen, by surface analysis, cuoio + ame.

parole.significato: the complex of heart, lungs, liver, and spleen
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *corāta, plural of *corātum, derived from Latin cor (“heart”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cornacla, alteration of Latin cornīcula, diminutive of cornīx.
From Vulgar Latin *eccum istaei, (genitive-)dative of *eccum iste. Compare Romanian acestei, Old French cestei.
From Vulgar Latin *eccum istorum, genitive(-dative) plural of *eccum iste.
From Vulgar Latin *eccum istūi, (genitive-)dative masculine singular of *eccum iste, from Latin eccum + istī, influenced by cui (“to whom”). Compare Romanian acestui, Old French cestui.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccum istāc, from eccum + istāc.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccum istīc, from eccum + istīc.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccum sīc. By surface analysis, ecco + sì. Closely parallel to Dalmatian coisa, Friulian cussì, Istriot cussèi, Sardinian gósi (bosìe, deàsi, etc.), Venetan cusì. Compare also Catalan així, French ainsi, Portuguese assim, Spanish así, Romanian așa, Sicilian accussì.
From Vulgar Latin *eccum tālis.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *(ec)cu tantum, from Latin eccum + tantum (“so much”).
From earlier cotevesto, contracted from a Vulgar Latin introductory locution *eccum tibi istum (literally “here [is] that [thing] for you”).

parole.significato: they; them; these people (used to indicate people close to the speaker)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *eccum tibi istōrum. Compare costoro and codesto.

parole.significato: he; him; this man (used to indicate a person close to the speaker)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *eccum tibi istūi. Compare costui and codesto.
Contracted from a Vulgar Latin introductory locution *eccum tibi istum (literally “here [is] that [thing] for you”).
From Vulgar Latin *cutica, derived from Latin cutis (“skin”).

From cotogno (“quince tree”), or less likely a Vulgar Latin root cotōnea, taken as a feminine singular from the plural of Latin cotōneum, ultimately from Ancient Greek κυδώνιον (kudṓnion). Also possibly from mela cotogna, from Latin māla cotōnea, also a feminine singular from the plural of mālum cot
Probably from Vulgar Latin *cocia (“pate, head”), from Latin cochlea (“snail”); compare coccia.
From Vulgar Latin *ācrispīnum (literally “sharp-thorned”), calqued from Ancient Greek ὀξυάκανθα (oxuákantha).
From Vulgar Latin *crina, from Latin crinis.
From Vulgar Latin *corrotulum, from Late Latin rotulus (cf. also Italian rocchio), rotula, diminutive of Latin rota.
From Vulgar Latin *crodius, from Gaulish *croudis (“hard”), from Proto-Celtic *kroudis, from Proto-Indo-European *krewh₂-.
Uncertain. Perhaps from Vulgar Latin *corrutulāre, frequentative of Latin corruere. If so, cognate with French crouler.

parole.significato: to roar (of rain or falling water)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cruscīre, from Frankish *krustijan. Otherwise is just another onomatopoeic word. Compare Spanish crujir, Old French croissir
Probably from a Vulgar Latin corūna, from Classical Latin corōna (“garland, wreath, crown”), whence also Italian corona.
Probably from Vulgar Latin *cattulus (“whelp, puppy”), from Latin catŭlus (“puppy”). Compare with Portuguese cachorro.
From a Vulgar Latin root *cōsīre, from *cōsere, from Latin cōnsuere.

From Vulgar Latin *cunla, syncopated form of cūnula, diminutive of Latin cūna, cūnae (“cradle”), from Proto-Italic *koinā, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱoyneh₂, derived from the root *ḱey- (“to be lying down; to settle”). Doublet of cuna.
From Vulgar Latin *corem m, from Latin cor n.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin cupiditia (from cupiditās), see -igia. Doublet of cupidità.
From Vulgar Latin *dantiāre. Documented since the thirteenth century.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dēcadere, from Latin dēcidere.
From Vulgar Latin *deexcitāre, derived from Latin excitāre (“to call forth, to rouse”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dia, first-declension reshaping of Classical Latin diēs. Doublet of die.

From a Vulgar Latin derivative of Late Latin ieiūnāre, from Latin ieiūnus, with the initial Latin ie- probably changing to de- and later di- in Italian. Compare English jejune, Catalan dejunar, Spanish ayunar, French jeûner, Portuguese jejuar, Old Italian giunare.
From Vulgar Latin, from Latin ieiūnus. The Latin derives from Proto-Italic *jagjūnos, itself from Proto-Indo-European *Hyeh₂ǵ-yu-, adjectival form of *Hyeh₂ǵ-ye/o- (“to sacrifice”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dismenticāre.

parole.significato: to wind (a skein) into a ball
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *dēpānāre, from Latin pānus (“thread wound upon the bobbin”), from Ancient Greek πῆνος (pênos). Compare Spanish devanar, Portuguese dobar, Catalan debanar, Sardinian demanare, Romanian depăna.

parole.significato: to depend (on something), to be up to (someone), to hang (on), to come from, to be due to
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dēpendĕre, from Classical Latin dēpendēre. By surface analysis, di- + pendere.
From dipingere (“to paint”). Possibly corresponds to a Vulgar Latin *dēpinctus for Latin dēpictus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin dē post, whence dopo. By surface analysis, univerbation of di + poi.
From Vulgar Latin *dērēctus or *dirictus, both assimilated forms from Latin dīrēctus. Doublet of diretto.
From di- + rupe, possibly corresponding to a Vulgar Latin *derupāre, from Latin rupes. Cf. also Portuguese and Galician derrubar, Sicilian sdirrupari.

From Vulgar Latin *dissēperāre, from Late Latin dissēparāre, from Latin dis- + sēparō. Cognate to Bourguignon dessevrai, Old French dessevrer, Asturian dixebrar, Old Spanish dessebrar. Cf. also Galician xebrar, Old Spanish exebrar, Occitan sebrar, French sevrer. Compare also separare.
From Vulgar Latin *disdignāre, reshaping of Latin dēdignārī (“disdain, scorn”), derived from dignus (“worthy”).
From Vulgar Latin *dispretiāre, derived from Latin pretium. Compare also disprezzare.

parole.significato: to despise, to scorn, to disdain, to slight
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *dispretiāre, derived from Latin pretium. Compare Portuguese desprezar, Spanish despreciar. See also deprezzare, from Latin depretio.

parole.significato: to destroy, wipe out or ruin
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *destrugere, from Classical Latin dēstruō, from dē- (“un-, de-”) + struō (“to build”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dolia, derived from Latin dolor. Compare Sicilian dogghia, Friulian dulie.
From the Vulgar Latin de unde (“from where, whence”), from Latin dē + unde (“whence”).
Possibly from Vulgar Latin *dēundulāre, with onomatopoetic influence of don (“dong (sound of a bell ringing)”).
From earlier dopoi, dipoi, inherited from Vulgar Latin dē post.
From Vulgar Latin dossum, from Latin dorsum. Doublet of the borrowed dorso.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dīrēctiāre.

From Vulgar Latin *dunquam, a cross of Late Latin dunc and Latin unquam (“ever”), with the former itself being a cross of Latin tunc (“then”) with dum (“while”). The final /-e/ may reflect an older form */ˈdonkwas/, with adverbial /-s/, for which cf. Middle French doncques.
From Vulgar Latin *eblum, syncopated form of Latin ebulum.
From Vulgar Latin *implīre~*implĕre, from Latin implēre.
From Vulgar Latin *ergere, from Latin ērigere. Doublet of erigere, which was borrowed.
From Vulgar Latin *erctus, equivalent of Latin ērectus, past participle of ērigō. Compare Spanish yerto. See also Italian eretto, a borrowing from Latin.
With gender shift, from Vulgar Latin *esclus, from Latin aesculus. See also eschio, with the same meaning.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *esclus, from Latin aesculus.
From faggio + -eto, possibly corresponding to a Vulgar Latin *fāgētum, from Latin fāgus. Compare Romanian făget, Spanish hayedo.
Diminutive of Vulgar Latin *facus, from Latin fascis (“bundle of wood”), or perhaps from Ancient Greek φάκελος (phákelos, “bundle”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fagīna.

parole.significato: to arm with scythes or sickles
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin falcāre, derived from Latin falx (“sickle, scythe”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *falciāre (compare French faucher), from Latin falx (“sickle, scythe”), from Proto-Indo-European *dhalk-, *dhalg- (“a cutting tool”).

parole.significato: to miss, to not hit (a target, a ball, etc.)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *fallīre, from Latin fallere.
From Vulgar Latin *fallita, derived from Classical Latin fallō (“to deceive; to be mistaken”).
From Vulgar Latin *fangus ~ *fanga (“mud”) of Germanic origin, see there for more. Compare French fange f and Spanish fango m.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *farrum, from Latin far (“emmer”).
From Vulgar Latin Fāta (“goddess of fate”), from the plural of Latin fātum (“fate”). Compare Catalan, Occitan, and Portuguese fada; French fée; Spanish hada.
From Vulgar Latin *fatīga, from Latin fatīgō (“to tire, weary”).

Diminutive of fazzolo, fazzuolo, itself from Vulgar Latin *faciolum, from Latin facies (“face”). Compare Romansh fazielet, fazalet, Swiss-German Fazaneetli, Friulian façolet, Venetan fasołeto, Istriot fassulito, Sicilian fazzulettu.
From Vulgar Latin, Late Latin faecia, faecea, from Latin faex.
From Vulgar Latin ferrāmenta, from the plural of Latin ferrāmentum.
From Vulgar Latin *fervere, from Classical Latin fervēre, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrewh₁- (“to be hot, boil”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *festizāre. Derivable from festa + -eggiare.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fĕtĕre, from Latin fētēre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *flammizāre, from Latin flamma. Derivable from fiamma (“flame”) + -eggiare (verb-forming suffix).
From Vulgar Latin *flavus, metathesized form of *favlus, *favulus, diminutive of Latin favus (“honeycomb”).

parole.significato: to shove (something) in, to stick (something) in, to thrust in
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *fīg(i)cāre, frequentative based on Latin fīgō (“drive in, fix in place”).

parole.significato: to entrust (something to someone); see affidare
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *fīdāre, from Latin fīdere.
From Vulgar Latin *felem m or f, from Latin fel n.

From some such adjectival form as Vulgar Latin *fīnus, from Latin fīnis (“a boundary, limit”), whence Italian fine. The prepositional usage is directly paralleled in Latin fīne, fīnī (“up to, as far as”).

parole.significato: to come down in flakes (of snow)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *floccāre, from Latin floccus (“tuft”). By surface analysis, fiocco + -are. Compare Neapolitan scioccare.
From Vulgar Latin *flunda, metathesis of an earlier form *fundla, a contraction of *fundula, diminutive of Latin funda (“sling”). Compare French fronde, Sicilian ciunna, Asturian flonda.
From Vulgar Latin *flossum, from Latin fossula.

parole.significato: to become; (in a future sense) to be
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *fīre, from Latin fīerī (“to become, be”). Compare Romanian fi.
From Vulgar Latin fīctus, from Latin fīxus. Doublet of fisso.
From Vulgar Latin *focolarium. Cf. focolare. Cognate with Sicilian fucularu.

parole.significato: to provide with a drainage or sewerage system
parole.testo: Perhaps from a Vulgar Latin root *fundiāre, from Latin fundus.
Inherited from a Vulgar Latin *faula, syncopated form of Latin fābula (“narration”). Doublet of favola and fiaba.
From Vulgar Latin *fullāre (“to full”, verb), from Latin fullāre (“cloth-fuller”, noun).

From formica + -aio, possibly corresponding to a Vulgar Latin *formīcārium, from Latin formīca. Compare Spanish hormiguero, Portuguese formigueiro, Friulian furmiâr, Romanian furnicar, Catalan formiguer.
From Vulgar Latin *fortiāre, or by surface analysis, forza + -are.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *frāgula.
Probably from Vulgar Latin *fragina, from Latin frangere, frangō (“to break”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *friscum.
From Vulgar Latin *frictāre, the frequentative of Latin fricāre (“to rub”).

parole.significato: to sparkle, to fizz, to fizzle
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *frīctiāre, from Latin frīgō, with conflations from both fricō and frīgeō.
From Vulgar Latin *fūricāre, from Latin fūr.

parole.significato: a lantern used in nighttime bird hunting or fishing
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *furneolus, derived from Latin furnus (“oven”).
From Vulgar Latin *frustiāre (“break into pieces”), from Latin frustum (“bit, fragment”).
From Vulgar Latin *focīlis [petra], derived from Latin focus. Compare French fusil, Friulian fusîl, Piedmontese fusil.

parole.significato: to escape, run away, scurry away
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *fugīre, from Latin fugere, from Proto-Italic *fugiō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewg-. Cognate with Sicilian fùjiri.

parole.significato: to smoke, to give off smoke
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fūmizāre. Derivable from fumo + -eggiare.
From Vulgar Latin *furittum (“petty thief”), which is derived from Latin fūr (“thief”). Cognate to French furet (“ferret”), Sicilian furittu (“ferret”), Spanish hurón (“ferret”).
From Vulgar Latin *fūsticellus, diminutive of Classical Latin fūstis (“stick, staff, club”).
Diminutive of Vulgar Latin *garra. See also Cornish garr.
From Vulgar Latin ienuārius, from Latin Iānuārius.
From Vulgar Latin *germiniāre, from Latin germināre. Cognate to Italian germinare.
From a Vulgar Latin *iectus, alteration of Latin iactus.
From a Vulgar Latin *carilium, *carylium, derived from caryon, from Ancient Greek κάρυον (káruon). Cognate with Spanish garojo.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *glacium/a, from Latin glaciēs. Doublet of ghiaccio and glassa.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *glacium/a, from Latin glaciēs. Doublet of ghiaccia. Compare Sicilian chiatru.

An adjective (likely reflecting Vulgar Latin *gluttus) based on the nominative of Latin gluttō (“glutton”), itself a noun based on gluttiō (“to swallow”), possibly related to gula (“throat”, whence also the Italian gola). Doublet of ghiottone, from the Latin accusative gluttōnem. Cognate to French g
From Vulgar Latin glīrus (attested in the Appendix Probi), from Latin glīrem.
From Vulgar Latin *iacilium, from Latin iaciō.
Through Vulgar Latin *jilju, ultimately from Latin lilium, from Ancient Greek λείριον (leírion). Compare, e.g., loglio (“darnel”). Cognate with Sicilian gigghiu.
From Vulgar Latin ziniperus, from Latin iūniperus.

parole.significato: dewlap (pendulous skin under a bovine's neck)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *iugāria [pellis], perhaps an alteration (influenced by iugum (“yoke”)) of *iugulāria [pellis] (“[skin] of the throat”), derived from Latin iugulum (“throat”).
From giovine (“young”) + -ezza (“-ness”, suffix denoting a state of being). Less likely from a Vulgar Latin *juvenitia. Compare French jeunesse.

parole.significato: a dice with a tapering point that can be made to spin on its axis with the fingers
parole.testo: Probably from Vulgar Latin *gȳrulus, diminutive of gȳrus (“circle; circular motion”).
From Vulgar Latin (manum) gemella(m), which consists of Latin manus (“hand”) and gemella, female form of gemellus (“double, a pair of something”).

parole.significato: to drip (of an object that carries liquid)
parole.testo: From goccia + -are or a Vulgar Latin root *guttiāre, from *guttia, from Latin gutta.
From Vulgar Latin or Late Latin colfus, colphus, culfus, alteration of colpus, from Ancient Greek κόλπος (kólpos). Doublet of colpo.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *gurgus, from Latin gurges.
From Vulgar Latin *ga(v)ota. Attested from the 13th century.
From Vulgar Latin *gottus, from Latin guttus.
From earlier godoviglia (and influenced by gozzo), likely inherited from Vulgar Latin *gaudibilia, plural of an unattested *gaudibilis, from gaudeō (“to rejoice”) + -ibilis (“-able”).
From Vulgar Latin *graclu(s), syncopated form of Latin grāculus (“jackdaw”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *greh₂-k- (“croak”). Compare English grackle, Spanish grajo, and Portuguese gralho.

parole.significato: to accept (something) with pleasure, to welcome, to appreciate
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *grātīre, from Latin grātus.
Probably from a Vulgar Latin *graphiāre, from Latin graphium, and influenced by Italian graffa or Lombardic krāpho (“hook”).

parole.significato: hail, shower, flood, torrent (figurative, of abuse etc.)
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin root *grandeola, from Latin grandō.

From *cranclu(m), accusative singular of Vulgar Latin *cranclus, by metathesis and syncope from a Late Latin *cancrulus (compare attested Medieval Latin cancrulus), a diminutive of Latin cancer (“crab”). The Latin derives from Proto-Italic *kankros, dissimilation of *karkros (“enclosure”) (because t
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *crassia, derived from Latin crassus (“fat”).
Possibly from a Vulgar Latin *gregius, as in lana *gregia, from Latin grex.
From Vulgar Latin *creppea (“crib, manger, trough”), from Old Frankish *krippija, *kribbija (“crib, stall”), from Proto-Germanic *kribjǭ (“crib”). More at crib.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *crītāre with irregular voicing.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cruppus. Akin to gruppo.
From Vulgar Latin *cruppus, (cf. Renaissance Latin grupus).

parole.significato: to earn (a salary, a wage, etc.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *wadaniāre, of Germanic origin; from Frankish *waiþanōjan, *waiþanōn (“to hunt, graze”) (a calque of Latin petere). Compare French gagner, Catalan guanyar, Portuguese ganhar, Galician gañar, Galician ganar, Galician gadaña, Galician gadañar, cf. also Spanish ganar and Spa

From Vulgar Latin *uadam, *wadam, from Frankish *wad, from Proto-Germanic *wadą (“ford”), from Proto-Indo-European *wadʰom, *wh₂dʰóm (ultimately from the root *weh₂dʰ-). Compare French gué (“ford”), Catalan gual, Occitan ga. Other sources list it as deriving from Latin vadum, itself from the same Pr

parole.significato: cheek (the soft skin on each side of the face)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *guancia, borrowed from Lombardic *wankja, from Proto-Germanic *wangô (“cheek”). Compare Old High German wanga (modern German Wange). Doublet of gargia.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *werrizāre. Derivable from guerra (“war”) + -eggiare (verb-forming suffix).

From Vulgar Latin *gūfus, further variant of Late Latin būfus, ultimately onomatopoeic. Its probable regional (such as Faliscan or Sabellic) origin is evident in the medial -f-, which corresponds to Latin -b-. Cognate to Romanian buhă, Spanish búho, Portuguese bufo, all "eagle owl". The original ōn-
From Vulgar Latin *imparāre, from in- + parāre. Compare French emparer (“to seize”).

parole.significato: to fetter, to hobble (a horse or other animal)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *impastoriāre, derived from Latin pāstōrius.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *impinctus, an alternative past participle of Latin impingō (instead of the Classical participle impāctus). Compare Catalan empenta, Old French empeinte.

parole.significato: to undertake, to embark on (an activity)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *imprehendere, from Latin prehendere.

parole.significato: to chase, to pursue, to follow closely, to press
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *incalciāre, derived from Latin calx (“heel”).

parole.significato: to charge, to entrust, to ask, to give the task of
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *incarricāre. By surface analysis, in- + caricare.
From in- + catenare, possibly also corresponding to a Vulgar Latin *incatēnāre, from Latin catēnāre. Compare French enchaîner, Spanish and Occitan encadenar, Portuguese encadear, Friulian incjadenâ.
By surface analysis, in- + cavalcare. Corresponds to Vulgar Latin *incaballicāre.

parole.significato: to direct (one's steps, one's gaze, effort, criticism, etc.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *indīrēctiāre, from *dīrēctiāre, from Latin dīrēctus. Compare French adresser, Portuguese endereçar, Catalan endreçar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *indulcīre, derived from Latin dulcis (“sweet”, adjective). By surface analysis, in- + dolce + -ire.
From Vulgar Latin *indūtiāre, derived from Latin indūtiae (“truce; pause”).
Probably derived from Vulgar Latin *hirpicāre, derived from Latin hirpex (“harrow”), in the sense of "to clamber up (by clinging like a harrow's teeth)".
From Vulgar Latin *īnfrangere, from Latin īnfringere, from in + frangō.

parole.significato: to deceive, take in, mislead, hoodwink
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin ingannāre (attested in a gloss), from Latin ganniō. Compare Spanish engañar, Portuguese enganar.
From in- + alzare, possibly corresponding to Vulgar Latin *inaltiāre (compare Romanian înălța, Old French enhaucier, Occitan enauçar).
From Vulgar Latin īnsignāre (also present in Medieval Latin), from Latin signāre. For sense 3 compare Spanish enseñar.
From Vulgar Latin *īnsemel, which is a combination of Latin īnsimul and semel. See also French ensemble, Catalan ensems and Neapolitan nzieme.

From Vulgar Latin *interrāre (“to put into earth”), from Latin in (“in”) + terra (“earth”). Numerous cognates include English inter; French enterrer; Catalan, Galician, Portuguese, and Spanish enterrar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *intunicāre, from Latin tunicāre. By surface analysis, in- + tonaca + -are.

parole.significato: to wrap, to wrap up (not normally used in a figurative sense)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *involtāre, from Latin involūtāre, frequentative of involvō through its past participle involūtus.
From Vulgar Latin *involtus, from *involvitus or *involŭtus, for Latin involūtus.
From Vulgar Latin *isula, from classical Latin īnsula.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *laceum, from Latin laqueus. Doublet of lasso and lazo.
From Vulgar Latin *landa, from Gaulish *landā, from Proto-Celtic *landā. Compare French lande.
From Vulgar Latin *largīre, from Latin largīrī.

parole.significato: a food made of flat sheets of pasta alternated with condiments
parole.testo: Possibly from Vulgar Latin *lasania, from Latin lasanum (“cooking pot”), from Ancient Greek λάσανον (lásanon, “trivet or stand for a pot”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *lavativus, derived from Latin lavō (“to wash”). Compare French lavatif.
From Vulgar Latin *lapideum, neuter substantivized form of Latin lapideus (“stony”), derived from lapis (“stone”).

From Vulgar Latin *illae, a nonstandard form of Latin illī (dative singular of illa). The ae in illae is modelled under influence of the dative case for first-declension feminine nouns, e.g. Classical Latin puellae. Cognate with Sicilian ci.
From Vulgar Latin *lenticla, syncopated form of Latin lenticula, diminutive of lēns.
Perhaps from a Vulgar Latin form *hirceus (“hircine”, “pertaining to goats”), derived from Latin hircus (“goat”), with an initial -l- attached from a preceding article.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *levāmen.
From Vulgar Latin *levātīcius, from Latin levāre. By surface analysis, levato + -iccio.
From Italian lezzare, apheresis of Italian olezzare (“to stink”), from Vulgar Latin *olidiāre, derived from Latin olidus (“emitting a smell”).
From Vulgar Latin *levĭtum (“yeast, sourdough”), from Latin levātus (“lifted”).

From Vulgar Latin *līsius, from Ancient Greek λισσός (lissós, “smooth”). Or, from *lixus, derived from *lixāre (“to clean, boil”), presumably related to lixa (“lye”). Compare Portuguese and Spanish liso, French lisse, Catalan llis, Sicilian lisciu, Friulian, Lombard, and Provençal lis, Romansh glisc
From Vulgar Latin *lista, of Germanic origin, from either Frankish *līsta or Lombardic līsta, both from Proto-West Germanic *līstā.
Deverbal from livellare (“to level, to make level”) + -o. Alternatively, from Vulgar Latin *lībellus.

parole.significato: the form of il that is used before the so-called impure consonants, that is, s+consonant (impure s), gn, pn, ps, x, y,…
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *(il)lu, from Latin illum, illud, by dropping il- and -m. Cognate with Sicilian lu.
From the Vulgar Latin *longitānus, from Latin longe; cognate with French lointain, Sicilian luntanu, Friulian and Romansch lontan, Dalmatian luntun.
From a Vulgar Latin variant of Latin lutra.

parole.significato: term used in the Middle Ages to describe a type of wild cat, possibly a lynx or leopard (cf. Portuguese onça)
parole.testo: Probably from Vulgar Latin *luncea, from Latin lynx, whence also Italian lince (a borrowed doublet). Cognate to French once.
From the older form oppio with concretion of the initial article, ultimately from Vulgar Latin *oplus < Latin opulus. Compare Sicilian loppiu.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *lūcicāre, from Latin lūcēre, lūx.
From Vulgar Latin *luciniōlum < *lucinium, alteration of Late Latin licinium (influenced by lūx (“light”)), from ellychnium, from Ancient Greek. Compare French lumignon.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *lūcōrem, from Latin lūceō.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin limāca, from Latin līmāx. See also limaccia.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *lūpum, from Latin lŭpum. Doublet of lupus and lovo.
From Vulgar Latin *lusciniolus, derived from Latin luscinia.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *macla, from Latin macula. Doublet of macula, a borrowing.
From Vulgar Latin *maclāre, from Latin maculāre.
From Vulgar Latin machineum, from Latin machina (“machine”), in the sense of a millstone of a mill.
From Vulgar Latin *madi(g)a, from magida, from Ancient Greek μαγίδα (magída). Compare Sicilian majiḍḍa.
From Vulgar Latin *mahanare, probably of Germanic origin and akin to Proto-Germanic *maidaz (“wounded, hurt”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *manianus, derived from Vulgar Latin *mania (“manual skill”), from Latin manus (“hand”).
From Vulgar Latin *amandula, from Latin amygdala, from Ancient Greek ἀμυγδάλη (amugdálē).
From Vulgar Latin *amandulus, from Latin amygdalus, from Ancient Greek ἀμύγδαλος (amúgdalos), ἀμυγδάλη (amugdálē).

parole.significato: to use with a technical purpose; to handle
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *manizāre (“handle”). Derivable from mano (“hand”) + -eggiare (verb-forming suffix). Cognate with Sicilian manijari.

parole.significato: used with animal names to indicate a person who changes shape into that animal; were-
parole.testo: Originally a Southern derivation of Vulgar Latin *hominārius, derived from Latin homō (“human”).
From Vulgar Latin *manibella or *manubella, from manus (“hand”).
From Vulgar Latin *mānsus, back-formed from Latin mānsuētus.
From Vulgar Latin *moruca, ultimately of Celtic origin.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *massīcius, from Latin massa. By surface analysis, massa + -iccio.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *mattaris, from Latin mataris (“javelin, pike”) (also materis, madaris or matara), of Celtic/Gaulish origin.
From Vulgar Latin *mattea (compare French masse, Spanish maza, Portuguese maça), probably vulgarly formed from Latin mateola (“hoe”). Cf. also Latin matia.

From earlier *metesimo, from Vulgar Latin *metipsimus, from a previous form *metipsissimus, derived from Latin -met (emphatic suffix) + ipse (“himself”) + -issimus (superlative suffix). Cognate with French même, Spanish mismo, Portuguese mesmo.
From the variant melagranata, from Vulgar Latin *melum granatum (cf. Italian melogranato, melograno), from Latin mālogrānātum or mālagrānātum.
From earlier melica, from Vulgar Latin melica, from Latin medica (“Median”). Compare Catalan melca.
From Vulgar Latin *melus, from Latin mālus.
From melogranato, from Vulgar Latin *melum granatum, from Latin mālogrānātum or mālagrānātum.
Probably from Vulgar Latin *minuus, having the same root as minuō (“to make smaller, to diminish”).
From mentire + -tore, possibly corresponding to a Vulgar Latin *mentitōrem, from Latin mentior. Compare French menteur, Romanian mințitor.

From a Vulgar Latin *mentionia, probably from a crossing of Latin mentiōnem with mentīri, or derived from a Late Latin mentiō (“lie”), itself probably from a hypothetical *mentītiō from mentītus, past participle of mentior. From Vulgar Latin *mixticāre, derived from Latin mixtus (“mixed”).

parole.significato: a very small amount of something
parole.testo: Probably derived from mica (“breadcrumb, morsel”). Alternatively from Vulgar Latin *miccus. Compare Corsican micca, Sicilian nicu and Sicilian miccu, Aromanian njic, Romanian mic.
From Vulgar Latin *melem m or f, from Latin mel n. Compare Sicilian meli, Romanian miere.
From Vulgar Latin *mināciāre, from Latin minācia, from mināx (“threatening”). Or, by surface analysis, minaccia + -are.
From Vulgar Latin *mina, Gaulish *meina (see also Welsh mwyn, Middle Irish míanach (“ore”)), from Proto-Celtic *meinis (“ore, metal”).

parole.significato: to chop, to mince, to dice, to grind, to crush
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *minūtiāre, derived from Classical Latin minūtia (“smallness; small thing, trifle”).
From Vulgar Latin *muccicāre, from the same Latin source as moccio (“snot”).
From Vulgar Latin *mucceus, from Latin mūcus, from Proto-Indo-European *mew-k- (“slimy, slippery”).

parole.significato: candle-end; top part of a wick
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *mŭcculus, a diminutive of Latin mŭccus, variant of mūcus.
From a variant of Late Latin modulus.
From a Vulgar Latin *mūtiliōnem, variant of *mūtuliōnem, from Latin mūtulus. Compare French moellon; cf. also Spanish mojón.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *mulgere, from Latin mulgēre (“to milk”).

parole.significato: crumb, breadcrumb (soft internal portion of bread)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *mollīca, derived from Latin mollis (“soft”). Cognate with Sicilian muḍḍica.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *montāre, from Latin montem (“mountain”). By surface analysis, monte + -are.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *multōnem, from Gaulish, from Proto-Celtic *molto-.

parole.significato: mulberry (fruit); fruit of a plant of the genus Morus
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *mōra, from Latin mōrum (whose plural was reanalyzed as the feminine singular), probably from Ancient Greek μόρον (móron).
From Vulgar Latin it *amurcla < *amurcula, from Latin amurca, from Ancient Greek ἀμόργη (amórgē), from ἀμέργω (amérgō, “pluck, pull”).
From a Vulgar Latin root *mordacia (< Latin mordax), probably altered to a form *mordacula from influence from tenacula. Compare French mordache, Portuguese mordaça, Spanish mordaza.
From Vulgar Latin *mordĕre, from Latin mordēre.
From Vulgar Latin *mortus, from Classical Latin mortuus, from Proto-Italic *mortwos, from Proto-Indo-European *mr̥twós, derived from the root *mer- (“to die; to disappear”).
From Vulgar Latin *mutius, from Latin mutilus. Compare French mousse and Spanish mocho.

parole.significato: to escape, to slip away, to slip through someone's fingers
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *muciāre, of Gaulish origin, from Proto-Celtic *mūk- (“to hide, stifle”), perhaps Proto-Indo-European *(s)mewk- (“to release, let loose, slip away”) or *(s)mewgʰ- (“to conceal”). Inherited from Vulgar Latin *mūgō (cf. French muge), a noun based on Latin mūgil (“mullet”).

parole.significato: to whimper or whine (of an animal)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *mūgulāre, from Latin mūgilāre. See also mugghiare.
From Vulgar Latin mungere, from Classical Latin mulgēre (“to milk”), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *h₂melǵ-.
From Vulgar Latin *movĕre, from Latin movēre.
From Vulgar Latin *muxinus, from Ancient Greek μυξῖνος (muxînos, “a kind of mullet”).
From Vulgar Latin *nappus (> Medieval Latin nappus), from Gothic *𐌷𐌽𐌰𐍀𐍀𐍃 (*hnapps), from Proto-Germanic *hnappaz (“cup, bowl”). Cognate with English nap (“bowl, cup”).
From Vulgar Latin *natica, from Latin natis (“buttock”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *nemīca, from ne- + mīca. Compare Old Venetan nemiga and Romanian nimic.
From Vulgar Latin *nespirum, from Latin mespilum, from Ancient Greek μέσπιλον (méspilon). Compare Portuguese nêspera and Spanish níspero.
From Vulgar Latin *nittus, a syncopation of Latin nitidus. Doublet of nitido, which is borrowed.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *nivāre. By surface analysis, nev(e) (“snow”) + -are (1ˢᵗ conjugation verbal suffix).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *nivicāre, a verb based on Latin nivem (“snow”, noun). By surface analysis, neve + -icare. Cognate with Sicilian nivicari.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *niblus, syncopated form of Latin nibulus, from an alteration of Latin milvus.
Probably imitative of infantile language, possibly through a Vulgar Latin *ninnus. Compare Spanish niño.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *(hin)nītrīre, variant of Vulgar Latin *hinnītīre, from hinnītus, perfect passive participle of hinniō (“to neigh”).
From Vulgar Latin *nuceola, from nuceus (“of nuts”), from Latin nux (“nut”). Compare Ligurian nisêua, Sicilian nuzzola, Venetan noxeła, Romansh nitschola, and also French noisette.
Derived from Vulgar Latin nōscum, from Latin nōbīscum (“with us”).
From Vulgar Latin *nōvāgintā, from Latin nōnāgintā (blended with novem (“nine”)), from earlier *nūnāgintā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥(d)ḱomt (“nine tens”).
From Vulgar Latin *novella, substantivized neuter plural form of Latin novellus (“new, novel”). Compare French nouvelle.
Through a dissimilated Vulgar Latin form *nuberāre, from Latin numerāre. Compare numerare.
From Vulgar Latin *noptiās, from Latin nuptiās.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *nocĕre, from Latin nocēre.
From Vulgar Latin *nŏra, from Late Latin nura, from Classical Latin nurus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *snusós.

From Vulgar Latin *oculāta, ultimately from Latin oculus (“eye”). Or by surface analysis, occhio + -ata.
From Vulgar Latin oclus, syncopated from Latin oculus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃okʷ-, *h₃ekʷ- (“eye; to see”). Doublet of oculo, a borrowing.
From Vulgar Latin *offerīre, from Latin offerre.
From Vulgar Latin *olidiāre, derived from Latin olidus (“emitting a smell”).

From Vulgar Latin *ōrulāre, from *ōrula, diminutive of Latin ōra (“border, margin”). Compare French ourler, Portuguese orlar and Spanish orlar.

parole.significato: border, edge, margin, brink, verge; the milled edge of a coin
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *orulus, diminutive of ōra.

parole.significato: to follow the tracks (of an animal)
parole.testo: From orma + -are, perhaps connected to a Vulgar Latin root *osmāre, ultimately from Ancient Greek ὀσμή (osmḗ). Compare Romanian urma.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *hormizāre.

parole.significato: to haul off, to luff, to come around (to steer into the wind)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *ortiāre (“to elevate, raise”), from Latin orior (“to rise”).
From Vulgar Latin *hordeāta, or a later formation with orzo + -ata. Compare French orgeat.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ossāmen, a collective derived from Latin os (“bone”). First attested in Dante. Synchronically derivable from osso (“bone”) + -ame (collective suffix).
From Vulgar Latin *pariolum, diminutive of *parium, from Transalpine Gaulish parios, from Proto-Celtic *kʷaryos (“cauldron”). Compare Welsh pair and Irish coire.

parole.significato: board for use in construction, scaffolding or furniture-making
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin palanca, from Latin phalanga, from the accusative form of Ancient Greek φάλαγξ (phálanx, “log, trunk, body of soldiers, etc.”). Doublet of the borrowing falanga and related to falange (“phalanx”).
From Vulgar Latin pānucla ← pānucula, modification of Latin pānicula, from pānus. Compare Spanish panoja, panocha.

First element from Vulgar Latin *patta (“paw, foot”), from Frankish *patta (“paw, sole of the foot”), from Proto-Germanic *pat-, *paþa- (“to walk, tread, go, step”), of uncertain origin and relation. From Vulgar Latin *papāverum, from Latin papāver (“poppy”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *papērium, from Latin papȳrius.
From Vulgar Latin *papīlum, from Latin papȳrus.

From Vulgar Latin *paraula, from Late Latin paravola, from Latin parabola (“comparison; later, speech”), from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ). Doublet of parabola, a borrowing. Compare with French parole, Catalan paraula, Sicilian palora and parola, Spanish palabra.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin pascua, from Latin pascha (influenced by pascuum, pascua (“grazing”)), from Ancient Greek πάσχα (páskha), ultimately from Hebrew פֶּסַח (pésakh, “Passover”). The surname was given to someone who was born this day.
From Vulgar Latin *passāre, derived from Latin passus (“step”, noun).
From Vulgar Latin *pastīcius, from Late Latin pasta, from Ancient Greek παστά (pastá).

parole.significato: to undergo, to receive, to endure
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *patīre, from Latin patī.
From Vulgar Latin *pavōrōsum, derived from Latin pavōrem (“fear”, noun). By surface analysis, paura + -oso.
From Vulgar Latin *paventāre, derived from pavēns, present active participle of paveō (“to be struck with fear; to fear”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pedicullus (with northern influences), from Latin pediculus (“footstalk”), a diminutive ultimately derived from Latin pēs (“foot”).
From Vulgar Latin *piltrum, of uncertain origin.
From Vulgar Latin *pinnaclum, from Late Latin pinnāculum, from Latin pinna. Diminutive of penne. Doublet of pinnacolo, and also panache.
From Vulgar Latin *pēnellus, diminutive of pēnis (“tail”).
Of Central Italian origin (given by the -nd- > -nn- assimilation, compare Italian annare) from Vulgar Latin *pendicāre, from Latin pendere (“hang”).

From a Vulgar Latin *pinta, alternative form of Latin picta (“painted [pot]”), feminine perfect passive participle of pingō (“to decorate; to paint”), from the custom of decorating crocks and pots by painting them.
Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *pendiolus or *pendiulus, from Latin pendulus.
From Vulgar Latin *pira, from the plural of Latin pirum, reanalyzed as a feminine singular.

Univerbation of per (“for”) + che (“which”), probably inherited from Vulgar Latin. Compare Neapolitan pecché, Sicilian pirchì, and further Romance parallels such as Sardinian pro chite, French pourquoi, Spanish porque/por qué, Portuguese porque/por que.
From Vulgar Latin *persequīre, from Latin persequī.
Deverbal from pertugiare + -o, from Vulgar Latin *pertūsiāre, from Latin pertūsus (“perforated”). Cognate with Sicilian pirtusu. Nowadays affricate pronunciation is a result of hypercorrection.
From Vulgar Latin *pessica (cf. Medieval Latin pesca), from Late Latin persica, from Latin persicum (“peach”, literally “fruit from Persia”). Compare French pêche.

parole.significato: the quantity of fish caught in a given amount of time; catch
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *piscātu, from Latin piscātus (“fished”), perfect active participle of piscor (“to fish”).
From Vulgar Latin *pessicus, from Latin persicus. Doublet of persico.
From Vulgar Latin *pēsum, from Latin pēnsum.

parole.significato: to pick (grapes) one by one (off a bunch, in order to eat them)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pilūc(i)cāre, ultimately from Latin pilāre.
From Vulgar Latin *pīnuculus, from pīnus (“pine”) + -culus (diminutive suffix).
