Inherited from Vulgar Latin *podiolum, diminutive of Latin podium. Cognate of Lombard pogioeul and Piedmontese pugiöl.
From Vulgar Latin *pos, from Classical Latin post. Compare Portuguese pois, Spanish pues, French puis, and Romanian apoi / Romanian poi (archaic păi).
Uncertain. Possibly from Vulgar Latin *pulliana, from Latin pullus (“chicken”, whence pollo), via a non-Tuscan variety. Compare Venetan pója.
From Vulgar Latin *pulliter, derived from Latin pullus (“young animal”).
From Vulgar Latin *punctiāre, from Latin punctus. Compare Spanish punzar, Catalan punxar, Portuguese punçar.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin puppa (“breast, teat, nipple, boob”), from Latin puppa, variant of pupa (“girl; doll”). Doublet of pupa.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *porcīle. By surface analysis, porco (“pig”) + -ile (“place for keeping”).

parole.significato: can, could; to be able to
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin potēre, regularization of Latin posse.
From Vulgar Latin praeceptum, form of praecipere (“to teach”), from Latin prae (“pre-”) + capere (“take”).
From Vulgar Latin *praedāre, from Latin praedārī.
From Vulgar Latin *praegnus < Latin praegnāns or praegnas.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pressō, from Latin presse (“narrow, short”). Cognate with Walloon and French près.
From Old Italian preite, from Vulgar Latin *previter, from Latin presbyter, from Ancient Greek πρεσβύτερος (presbúteros). Compare French prêtre, Romanian preot.

From Vulgar Latin *prōda, from Latin prōra (via dissimilation), borrowed from Ancient Greek πρῷρα (prōîra), from Proto-Indo-European *pro-, form of *por-. Doublet of prua and prora. Compare Spanish proa.
From Vulgar Latin *proexsūcāre, from Late Latin exsūcāre (“to extract”).
From asciutto (“dry”), with a change of prefix, or perhaps from a Vulgar Latin *perexsūctus, from Latin per + exsūctus. Compare Portuguese presunto.
From Vulgar Latin *prūdere, with dissimilation and a change in conjugation from Latin prūriō (“to itch or tingle”).
From Vulgar Latin *prūnea, from Vulgar Latin *prūna, feminine singular formed from the neutral plural of Latin prūnum, from Ancient Greek προῦμνον (proûmnon). Cognate with Sicilian prunu.
From Vulgar Latin *pullētrus, from Latin pullus (“young animal”, whence Italian pollo), likely via a Gallo-Italic language, for expected polletro.
From Vulgar Latin *pūnctēculāre, from pungō.
From Vulgar Latin *pūtīre, from a change in conjugation of Latin pūteō (“to stink”), derived from a form *pūtos, from Proto-Indo-European *puHtós, derived from the root *puH- (“rotten, foul”).
From Vulgar Latin *putrīre, from Latin putrēre (with a change in conjugation class), with inflexions taken from putrēscere.

Said to come from Vulgar Latin *pūtium, derived from Latin pūteō. More likely from the elision of Latin put(i)du(s), which is from the same root and would also explain the etymon of its feminine counterpart.

From Vulgar Latin *eccum hāc. Related to Portuguese cá, Spanish acá, French çà, Sicilian cca. The original geminated -cc-, though lost in the standard language, is still found in most regional Italian varieties. Compare Sicilian cca.
Diminutive of quadro, perhaps corresponding to Vulgar Latin *quadrellus, from Latin quadrus. Compare French carreau, Spanish cuadrillo, Dalmatian cadrial.
From Vulgar Latin *quaresima, from Latin quadrāgēsima (“the fortieth part; Lent”), substantive of quadrāgēsimus (“fortieth”). Doublet of quadragesima, which was a borrowing.

parole.significato: used to refer to someone distant in terms of space or time from the speaker; that (person)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Italian quelli, via palatalization of /ll/ before /i/ (cf. begli < belli), from Vulgar Latin *eccum illī, alternative nominative singular of Vulgar Latin *eccum ille, from Latin eccum + ille.
Contracted from Vulgar Latin *eccum ille, from Latin eccum + ille.
From Vulgar Latin *eccum iste, from Latin eccum (deictic) + iste (“that”), the former surviving also as Italian ecco and the latter as esto.
From Vulgar Latin *eccum hīc (with apocope), from Latin eccum + hīc. The original geminated -cc-, though lost in the standard language, is still found in most regional Italian varieties.
From Vulgar Latin *eccum hince, the latter element a variant of Latin hinc (“hence, from here”).

From Vulgar Latin *eccum inde. The regular outcome of the stressed vowel should have been */e/. The actual /i/ may have been taken by analogy from quinci (< *eccum hince), with which quindi forms a natural pair, and where stressed /i/ is expected due to the following /ntʃ/ triggering anaphonesis.

parole.significato: used to denote several kinds of vegetables, especially a carrot
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rādica, from Latin rādīcula, diminutive of rādīx (“root”). Compare Sardinian rádica and Sicilian ràdica.
The feminized version of the masculine ragazzo (“boy; boyfriend”) from Vulgar Latin *ragatius, from Ancient Greek ῥάκος (rhákos, “rag, tatter”, suggesting the clothing).

From Vulgar Latin *raglāre, from *ragulāre, from Late Latin ragō (whence French raire, réer, Romanian rage). Compare Venetan rajar, ragiar, Sicilian ragghiari, French railler, Occitan ralhar, Catalan rallar. The form ragliare in Italian may have been influenced by a northern Italian variant or Gallo
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *arāmen, variant of Late Latin aerāmen, derived from Latin aer-.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rancicus, modified from Latin rancidus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rancius, from Classical Latin rancidus (“rancid, rank”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rānucula, a diminutive from Latin rāna (“frog”), with a masculine form later becoming more widespread; by surface analysis, rana + -occhio. Compare ranuncolo.
From Vulgar Latin *rapīre, from Latin rapere, from Proto-Italic *rapiō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rp-i-, from *h₁rep- (“to snatch”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rāsāre (cognate with French raser), a frequentative verb formed from Latin rāsus, past participle of rādō.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rāsclāre, syncopated form of *rāsculāre, from Latin rāsculum (“instrument for shaving”), from rāsus. Compare Occitan rasclar, French râler, racler.
From Vulgar Latin *raspāre, from Frankish *hraspōn.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin rattus (“rat”), from Proto-Germanic *rattaz.
From Vulgar Latin *recaptāre, from re- + captāre. Compare riscattare (“to ransom”).

parole.significato: to ask for, demand, apply for
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *requaerere, from Latin requīrere with dissimilation of /r–r/ to /d–r/, from re- with quaerere, from Proto-Indo-European.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *refrangere, from Latin refringere.
From Vulgar Latin *aurigalbulus (literally “golden-yellow bird”), derived from Latin aurum (“gold”) + galbulus (“yellow bird”).
Unknown. Perhaps from Vulgar Latin reprobitāre (contracted in *reprobtō, reprobtāre and with a replacement of ri- with rin-), intensive form of reprobō, reprobāre (“to reject, condemn”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *remurclum, from *remurculum, from Latin remulcum.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ringulāre, derived from Latin ringī.

parole.significato: to renounce (a doctrine, faith or ideal)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *renegāre, from Latin negāre. Compare French renier and Spanish renegar.
From the intermediate Vulgar Latin *ri(ji)one(m), from the masculinization of Latin regiōnem. Compare the borrowed doublet regione. Cognate with Sicilian rijuni.

parole.significato: to repent again or a lot
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *repaenitīre, or by surface analysis, ri- + pentirsi.

parole.significato: to climb again, to ascend again
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *resalīre. Synchronically derivable from ri- + salire.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *reexcaptāre, from Latin captāre. Compare Italian ricattare (“to blackmail”), Catalan and Spanish rescatar (“to rescue”), Portuguese resgatar (“to rescue”).
From Old Italian risco, from Vulgar Latin *resecum or deverbal from resecare, via risicare and later riscare, rischiare, both from Latin resecō (“to cut off”). Compare Sicilian rìsicu.

parole.significato: to turn or turn over again
parole.testo: Probably from ri- + voltare, or less likely from a Vulgar Latin root *revoltāre, from *revolvitāre, for *revolūtāre, as a frequentative of revolvō from its past participle Latin revolūtus.
From Vulgar Latin *rēctiāre, from Latin rēctus.

From Vulgar Latin rauba, of Germanic origin, via Gothic or Frankish *raub, all from Proto-Germanic *raubaz. Cognate with Sicilian robba, English robe, rob, and reave; and Scots reif (“robbery, stolen goods”).
First attested in 1465. From Vulgar Latin arrugia, of pre-Indo-European origin.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rōsicāre, frequentative based on Latin rōdere, whence Italian rodere.
From Vulgar Latin *rōsiclāre < *rōsiculāre, from *rōsicāre (cf. Italian rosicare), from Latin rōdō.

Probably from Vulgar Latin *boreārius, derived from Latin boreās (“north wind”), from Ancient Greek Βορέᾱς (Boréās). Reshaped by influence from rovo (“thorn”), because of the cold wind being perceived as stinging.

parole.significato: to pour, spill, damp, tip, shower, lay
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *reversiāre, modified from or cognate with Late Latin reversāre, a verb based on Latin reversus. Doublet of riversare, which was borrowed from Latin.

From Vulgar Latin *rubiculus, derived from Latin rubeus (“red”). A more normal outcome would have been *ruvecchio. The reason for there still being a /b/ is not clear, but influence from related words like robbio or rubino may have played a role.

Ultimately from Vulgar Latin *rōsāta, from Latin rōs, but borrowed, at least in the form rugiada, from some Gallo-Italic language. The form in question is first documented in the late thirteenth century, as are both of the more indigenous-looking variants above. More information As ⟨VgiV⟩ has since
From Vulgar Latin *r(īv)uscellum, double-diminutive from Latin rīvus (“river”). Compare French ruisseau.
From Vulgar Latin *roteolāre, from Latin rota. Cf. also sdrucciolare.
From Vulgar Latin *sabla, from a contraction of Latin sabula, plural of sabulum, variant of sabulō. Compare French sable, Occitan sabla.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *axālis. Doublet of assale and asciale.
Probably from a Vulgar Latin derivative of a crossing of Latin solidus with validus. Doublet of soldo, solido, and sodo.

Inherited from Old Italian sarpare, of uncertain further origin. Babiniotis considers the term to be from an earlier Vulgar Latin *ex-harpāre, which would be borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐξαρπάζω (exarpázō, “to snatch away from, tear out”), with sense development "to tear off" > "to drag quickly" > "
From Vulgar Latin *salsa, noun use of the feminine of Latin salsus (“salted”), from saliō, from sal.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sapēre, from Latin sapĕre (“taste, know”).
Compare saggio and savio, from Vulgar Latin *sapium.
From Vulgar Latin *sarclum, from Latin sarculum.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *batuaculum, with influence from bavaglio.

From Vulgar Latin *exbataculāre, from Early Medieval Latin bataculāre (“to yawn”), possibly by the intermediation of a Western Romance language (e.g. Old Occitan esbadalhar). The foreign origin could be indicated by the treatment of Latin -c'l- (the expected Tuscan outcome would have been *sbadacchi
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ēbriōnia, from ēbrius (“drunk”). Compare ubriaco and ebbro from the same root.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *excadēre (“fall out”), from Latin ex- + cadere.

parole.significato: to paw (beat the ground with the forefoot) [auxiliary avere] (of a horse)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *scalpitāre, frequentative of Latin scalpere (“to scratch”).
From Vulgar Latin *excampāre, variant of *excappāre, a verb based on Late Latin cappa (“cloak”).

parole.significato: to avoid, to evade, to escape (danger, a risky situation)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *excapulāre, from Late Latin capulāre, from Latin capiō. Compare Portuguese escapulir.
From the verb scapolare (“to avoid”), from Vulgar Latin *excapulāre, from ex- + capulus (“handle, halter”).

parole.significato: to run away, flee, escape, scarper or skedaddle
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *excappāre, a verb based on Late Latin cappa (“cloak”).

For Vulgar Latin *scarafaius (cf. 10th c. glosses scarafagius), a local, perhaps Oscanized variant of Latin scarabaeus (“scarab, dung beetle”), of uncertain origin. This variant is also reflected by several Provencal forms. Compare Sicilian scravagghiu and Venetan scarafajo.

parole.significato: to dishevel, to tousle, to ruffle (hair)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *excarmināre, from Latin ex- + carmināre (“to card”), from carmen (“card for wool”), and influenced by Italian scapigliare.

parole.significato: to till, to break up (the soil)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exquassāre, from Latin quassāre (“to shake repeatedly”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exēligere, from Latin ex (“out of, from”) + ēligere.

Past participle of scegliere, corresponding to a Vulgar Latin *exeltus, from *exelctus, from *exēlēctus, from Latin ex (“out of, from”) + ēlēctus (“picked, chosen, elected”). Compare Sicilian sceltu, scertu, Venetan sièlto, Friulian sielt; see also French élit.

parole.significato: to decrease, to reduce, to diminish
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *exsēmāre, from Latin sēmis (“a half”). Compare Sicilian scimuniri and scimunitu.
From Vulgar Latin *exsēperāre, derived from Latin sēparāre (“to separate”). Equivalent to s- + severare.

From a Vulgar Latin *sclacta, *slacta, derived from a Germanic language, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *slahtō, related to *slahaną (“to strike, hit”). Compare Judeo-Italian סְקֵילַאטַה (səqēlaʔṭâ /⁠schelatta⁠/). Cognate with Danish slægt (“family; lineage”), Dutch geslacht (“sex; gender; lineage;
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exaquāre, a verb based on Latin ex- (“out”) + aqua (“water”).
From sciame + -are. Less likely from Vulgar Latin *exāmināre, from Latin exāmen. Compare French essaimer, Spanish enjambrar, Portuguese enxamear, Venetan samar.
From a contraction of Vulgar Latin *exsapidus, restructuring of *exsipidus, whence Italian scipito.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exēlinguāre, from ex- + ēlinguō, derived from Latin ēlinguis.
From sciogliere, or Vulgar Latin *exsoltus, from exsolūtus.

parole.significato: to strike, to go on strike
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exoperāre, from ex- + operō.
From Vulgar Latin *exsìpidus (with a forward shift in stress), from Latin īnsipidus (with a change in prefix). Compare Sicilian scìpitu. Related also to the Italian sciap(id)o.
From Vulgar Latin *exsupāre, from Latin ex- + supāre. See also scipare.
Diminutive (see -olo) of earlier scoiatto, from scoriatto, from Vulgar Latin *scuriatus, from scurius, variant of Latin sciūrus.
From Vulgar Latin *excōlāre, from Latin cōlāre, or equivalent to Italian s- + colare. Compare French écouler, Spanish escolar, Portuguese escoar, Venetan scołar, Sicilian sculari.
From Vulgar Latin *excurtiāre, from Latin curtus. Compare Catalan escurçar.
From Vulgar Latin *excorrigō, from Latin ex- + corrigō (“to set right, straighten”), cognate with Old Spanish escurrir (“to accompany someone to say goodbye”).
From Vulgar Latin *excornum. By surface analysis, deverbal from scornarsi (“to make a fool of oneself”) + -o. Compare Neapolitan scuorno.
Probably from Vulgar Latin *excutulāre, from Latin excutere (cf. scuotere). Compare Romanian scutura.

parole.significato: to scorch, to singe, to burn, to scald
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *excoctāre, derived from Latin excoctus, perfect passive participle of excoquō (“to boil; to melt; to dry up”), derived from coquō (“to cook”).

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *scrībānem (with later change of declension), accusative of Latin *scrība, from Latin scrība (“writer, scribe”), with altered declension. Compare Occitan escrivan, French écrivain, Spanish escribano. Doublet of scriba.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *scuticium, from Latin scutica.
From Vulgar Latin *exquatere, *excotere, a remodelling of Latin excutere on simplex quatere. Compare Romanian scoate (“remove”). Cf. also escutere, a borrowed doublet.
Ultimately from Vulgar Latin *excorrigiāta, but likely borrowed through another language such as Venetan scuria.
Probably inherited from Vulgar Latin *exdēradiāre.

parole.significato: to slip, to slide (and fall, or risk falling) (of a person)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *exderoteolāre, from ex + de + roteolāre, from Latin rota (“wheel”). Cf. also ruzzolare.
From Vulgar Latin *siccāricius, from Latin siccus (“dry”). By surface analysis, secco + -ereccio.
From earlier *sequire, from Vulgar Latin *sequīre of deponent Classical Latin sequī, from Proto-Italic *sekʷōr, from Proto-Indo-European *sékʷetor, derived from the root *sekʷ- (“follow”).

parole.significato: to continue (one's work or studies, a speech, etc.)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *sequitāre (“follow”), from sequor (“to follow”) + -itō (frequentative suffix). See sequitus. Compare Sicilian sicutari.

From Vulgar Latin *sennus, of Germanic origin (whence also Old French sen, san (“mind, sense, direction”), Occitan sen, Catalan seny, Spanish sien), from Frankish *sinn (“sense, mental faculty, way, direction”), from Proto-Indo-European *sent- (“to go”). Akin to Old High German sinn (“mind, sense, j
Inherited from Vulgar Latin sepellīre~*sepullīre, from Latin sepelīre.
From Vulgar Latin *serrāre (“close, shut”), from Late Latin serāre (“to fasten, bolt”), from Latin sera (“bolt, cross-bar”).

By surface analysis, s- + faccia + -are, perhaps corresponding to a Vulgar Latin *exfaciāre, from Latin faciēs (“face, visage”). Parallel to, or cognate with, Old French esfacier. (The semantics, however, suggest separate developments.) Less likely related to Galician esfachar.

parole.significato: exhausted horseshoe; the old horseshoe after it is removed from the hoof of a horse
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *exferra. By surface analysis, deverbal from sferrare (“to unshoe (a horse)”) + -a. Compare Neapolitan sferra and Sicilian sferra.

parole.significato: to throw, hurl (with force yet precision)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *exferrāre. By surface analysis, s- + ferro (“horseshoe”), ferri (“shackles”) + -are. Cognate with Sicilian sfirrari.

parole.significato: to break down, to knock down, to break through
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exfundorāre, from *fundorem, analogical accusative derived from Latin fundus n (“bottom”).

parole.significato: to force (a door, a person to do something, etc.)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *exfortiāre, ultimately from Latin fortis (“strong”). Or, by surface analysis, s- + forza + -are.
From Vulgar Latin *sclembus, *slembus, borrowed from Gothic *𐍃𐌻𐌹𐌼𐌱𐍃 (*slimbs) or Frankish *slimb, both from Proto-Germanic *slimbaz. Unrelated to Ancient Greek σκιμβός (skimbós, “lame”).
Probably from Vulgar Latin *excommentāre, from ex- + commentārī (“to consider thoroughly”).

parole.significato: alternative form of siamo: inflection of essere:
parole.testo: Probably from an unattested Vulgar Latin *(es)sīre, from Vulgar Latin essere. Superseded by (originally Tuscany, archaic or Rome) semo.

From Vulgar Latin *singluttiāre, from singultiāre, from Latin singultāre, from singultus (“sobbing”). The (Vulgar) Latin was altered under the influence of gluttiō, gluttīre. Compare French sangloter. Compare also Portuguese soluçar, Romanian sughița, Spanish sollozar, from *suggluttiāre.

From Vulgar Latin *singluttium, ultimately from Latin singultus (“sobbing”), influenced by gluttiō (“to swallow”). Doublet of singulto. Cognate with French sanglot, Venetan sangiuto, among others. Compare also Portuguese soluço, Romanian sughiț, Spanish sollozo, Sicilian sugghiuzzu and suttugghiu, f
From Vulgar Latin *smeraldus, from Latin smaragdus, from Ancient Greek σμάραγδος (smáragdos) (modern, σμαράγδι (smarágdi)), of Semitic origin. Compare French émeraude.

parole.significato: to crumble, to mush, to squish
parole.testo: From s- + minuzzare, from Vulgar Latin *minūtiāre, from Latin minūtus.

parole.significato: to put out, to extinguish, to quench (a fire, hunger, thirst, enthusiasm, etc.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exmortiāre, from mortuus (“dead”).

parole.significato: to move (a heavy object) with effort or difficulty; to move; to shift; to dislodge
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *exmovĕre, from Latin ēmovēre. Compare French émouvoir and Sicilian smòviri.

From Vulgar Latin *snellus (“brisk, lively”) (compare Old French esnel, isnel (“sudden, quick”), Occitan isnel, irnel (“lively”)), from Frankish *snell, *snel (“sudden, quick”) from Proto-Germanic *snellaz (“active, sudden, quick”). Akin to Old High German snel, snell (“bold, agile, lively, swift, b

parole.significato: to stir up or incite (especially covertly)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *subilāre, from Latin sībilāre. sibilare and zufolare. Continued influence from the prefix so- < Latin sub- may have prevented fricativization of the original /-b-/.

parole.significato: help, aid, rescue, succour, assistance, relief
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *succursum, from Latin succursus. Compare French secours.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *suffertus, innovative past participle for Classical Latin sufferre. Compare Catalan sofert, French souffert, Old Spanish sufierto.
From Vulgar Latin *suffīctus, perfect passive participle of Latin suffīgō (“to fasten or fix onto”); compare Classical Latin suffīxus. Cognate with Piedmontese sofit.

parole.significato: to suffer, to feel, to go through
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *sufferīre, from Latin sufferre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *subdiurnāre, from Latin sub- (“under, a little over”) + Late Latin diurnus (“lasting for a day”). Cognate to English sojourn.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sōlātīvus. By surface analysis, sole + -ato + -io.

parole.significato: the gesture of shielding one's own eyes from sunlight by putting an open hand at the level of the eyebrows
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sōliculum.
Probably from Vulgar Latin *subliticāre, metathesized from *subtītillicāre, from Latin tītillāre. An alternative theory is metathesis from sollicitāre. Compare Sicilian accattigghiari.
From Vulgar Latin *similiantem, present participle of *similiāre, a verb based on Latin similis (“similar”). By surface analysis, somigliare + -ante.
From Vulgar Latin *similiāre, a verb derived from Latin similis (“similar”).

parole.significato: to drowse, to doze off, to nod off
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *somniculāre, derived from somniculus, diminutive of Latin somnus. Compare Latin somniculōsus, French sommeiller.

parole.significato: a singer, commonly a woman, with a register higher than alto and the rest of the parts: soprano leggero, soprano lirico
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *superānus, from Latin super. Also from *superānus: Italian sovrano.
From Vulgar Latin *sorbea, *sorba, from Latin sorbus (“tree of the genus Sorbus: service tree, rowan, etc.”). Related to sorbo.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sorbīre, from Latin sorbēre.
From Vulgar Latin *subrīdĕre, from Latin subrīdēre.
From Vulgar Latin, Late Latin sorsum, *sorpsum, from sorptum, from alteration of Latin sorbitum, supine of sorbeō (“to suck”).
From a Vulgar Latin *sorta, itself from Latin sortem, possibly through French sorte.
From Vulgar Latin *sortīre, from Latin sortīrī, as in Etymology 1.
From Vulgar Latin *surctus, analogically formed from the present stem of surgere, replacing surrēctus.
Feminine form of sottano (“lower”), i.e. "that which is worn underneath", perhaps from Vulgar Latin *subtāna, compare tana f (“lair, den”, noun).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *subtānus, from Latin subtus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *superculum. Compare Sicilian superchiu.
From Vulgar Latin *subrā, a variant of suprā either through intervocalic voicing or influenced by sub. Doublet of sopra- and sor-.
From Vulgar Latin *spatla, from Late Latin spatula, from Classical Latin spatha (“straight sword”). Compare spatola, a borrowed doublet.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin sparāniāre (attested in the Reichenau Glossary), from Frankish *sparanjan, from Proto-Germanic *sparāną (compare French épargner, English spare and Dutch/German sparen). Cognate with Sicilian sparagnari.
The modern sense of shooting derives jocularly from the older culinary sense, which is from Vulgar Latin *exparāre, formed as ex- (intensive prefix) + parō (“to prepare”).
From Vulgar Latin *expassāre, from expandō (“to stretch out”).

From Vulgar Latin *expaventāre, derived from the present participle of Classical Latin expaveō. Compare Spanish, Portuguese, Occitan, and Catalan espantar (also Catalan and Occitan espaventar); French épouvanter; Sicilian scantari; also Romanian înspăimânta.
From Vulgar Latin speclum, syncopated form of Latin speculum, from the verb speciō. Compare specolo, a borrowed doublet.
From Vulgar Latin *spiclu(m), contracted form of Latin spīculum, diminutive of spīcum, alternative form of spīca (“ear of grain”). Doublet of spigolo.
From Vulgar Latin *spinla, from contraction of Late Latin spīnula, diminutive of Latin spīna. Doublet of spinula, a borrowing.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *expingere, from Latin ex- + pangere.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *expinctus, past participle of *expingō, from Latin ex- + pangō.
From Vulgar Latin *spiō, from Frankish *spehō (“spy”), from Frankish *spehōn (“to spy”). By surface analysis, spiare (“to spy”) + -one.
Deverbal from squadrare + -a. May correspond to a Vulgar Latin *exquadra, from *exquadro, exquadrāre, from Latin ex- + quadrō, from quadrus. Compare French équerre.

parole.significato: to delimit in a square or rectangular shape
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *exquadrāre, derived from Latin quadrus. Compare French équerrer.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exquartiāre, from Latin quartus (“fourth”). Compare squartare (“to quarter”).

parole.significato: to quarter, to divide into quarters (also in reference to people; see draw and quarter)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exquārtāre, from Latin quārtus (“fourth”).

parole.significato: to put (animals) into a pen or fold (for the night)
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin *stablāre, from Latin stabulāre. By surface analysis, stabbio + -are. Doublet of stabulare, a borrowing.
From Vulgar Latin *stantia (“standing, stopping-place”), from Latin stantem, from stāre.

parole.significato: furniture of a locale where merchandise is stored and sold
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *usitilium, derived from Latin ūtēnsilia. Cognate with Sicilian stigghiu.
From Vulgar Latin *extorcere, ultimately from Latin torquēre. Doublet of estorcere, a borrowing from Latin.
Probably from a Vulgar Latin *exturdīre, from Latin turdus (“thrush”), or perhaps from s- + tordo. Compare French étourdir.

Uncertain. Some possibilities are presented below: * From Vulgar Latin *exturpiāre, from Latin ex- (“throughout; thoroughly”) + turpis (“ugly; unsightly”) + -are (infinitive suffix); literally, “to [make someone look] ugly throughout”, “to [render someone] thoroughly unsightly” (by maiming etc.). *
Probably a deverbal from *stosciare + -o coming from Vulgar Latin *extortiāre, which is ultimately derived from Latin tortus, past participle of torqueō (“to twist; to hurl”).

From Vulgar Latin *extractiāre, derived from Latin extractus, past participle form of extrahō (“to extract, remove”). Compare Sicilian strazzari, Venetan strasar, Occitan estraçar, Piedmontese strassé.
From Vulgar Latin *strambus, from Latin strabus, from Ancient Greek, akin to Albanian shtrembër, Romanian strâmb, Sicilian strammatu, Spanish zambo.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *strīdulāre, from strīdere (“to creak, screech etc.”).
From Vulgar Latin *strictiāre, from Latin strictus, past participle of stringō.

parole.significato: to brush, to rub (a body part, an object)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *extrūsciāre, inchoative form of Vulgar Latin *extrūsāre, from Latin extrūdō (“to drive out”) (infinitive extrūdere), perhaps influenced by strisciare (“to drag”). Cognate with Sicilian truscia and ntrusciari.
From Vulgar Latin *extūtāre, from Latin tūtārī (“avert, ward off”).

parole.significato: chisel (especially the sort used by stonemasons)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *subla, contraction of Latin sūbula.
From Vulgar Latin *sublum, syncopated form of *sūbulum, an aphaeretic form of Late Latin īnsūbulum, from Latin īnsuō + -bulum, or related to sūbula. Compare Romanian sul.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sūculare, *succulare, from sūcus (“juice, sap, moisture”), from Proto-Indo-European *suk-. Compare Latin sūgō (“suck”) (< Proto-Indo-European *sug⁽ʰ⁾-), Italian sucare.
From Vulgar Latin *sūgillum, from Latin sigillum. Doublet of sigillo.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sūberus, from Latin sūberem.
From Vulgar Latin *sola, from Latin solea. Compare Spanish suela, Portuguese sola.
From susino (“plum tree”), from Vulgar Latin *susīna, from Latin Sūsa (“ancient capital of Elam”).
From Vulgar Latin *susīna, from Latin Sūsa.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exvagāre, from Latin ēvagārī (“to wander off”), from vagor.

parole.significato: to disappear, vanish, take flight, get away or fade
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exvānīre, from Latin ēvānēscō with a change of prefix.
From Vulgar Latin *exvellere, from Latin ex- + vellere (“to pluck, stretch”). Piecewise doublet of evellere.
Past participle of svellere (“to pluck out, root out”), from Vulgar Latin *exvellere, from Latin vellere (“to pluck, stretch”), perhaps influenced by Spanish suelto (“free; agile”).

parole.significato: to foil, to thwart, to baffle
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *exventāre, a verb based on Latin ventus (“wind”). Compare Sicilian sbintari.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exvolāre, from Latin ex- + volāre. Compare Friulian svolâ.
From Vulgar Latin *tafānus, from Latin tabānus (“gadfly, horsefly”).

parole.significato: type of pasta originally from Abruzzo, Italy.
parole.testo: Adaptation of the Abruzzese dialectal word. May correspond to a Vulgar Latin *taliātīcius. By surface analysis, tagliato (“cut”) + -iccio.
From Vulgar Latin *tālōnis, from Latin tālus (“ankle”). Cognate with French talon.
Perhaps from Vulgar Latin *subtāna, compare sottana f (“lower”, adjective).

Possibly from Vulgar Latin *tastāre, from taxitāre, frequentative of Late Latin taxāre, from Classical Latin tangō (“to touch”). Compare Catalan, Occitan, and Venetan tastar; Old French taster; Friulian tastâ; Sicilian tastari.

parole.significato: loom, frame (frame in which to weave)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin or Medieval Latin *tēlārium, from Latin tēla.
From a Vulgar Latin root *templa, from *tempula, from Latin tempora, plural of tempus. Compare French tempe, Portuguese têmpora, Romanian tâmplă.
From Vulgar Latin *terrificāre, from Latin terrārī + faciō (“to make”).
From Vulgar Latin *testulum, diminutive of Latin testum (“earthenware pot, vessel”).
From Vulgar Latin *tegella, diminutive of Latin tegula, doublet with teglia (“baking tray”) and tegola (“roofing tile”).

parole.significato: to pull, to draw, to tug, to drag
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tīrāre.

parole.significato: to touch (to make physical contact with)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tuccāre, of Germanic or onomatopoeic origin.
From Vulgar Latin *tundus, back-derived from Late Latin retundus, whence older Italian ritondo. Compare Sicilian tunnu.
From Vulgar Latin *toppus, from Frankish *topp (“summit, top”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *torcĕre, from Latin torquēre.
From Vulgar Latin *torclāre, from Late Latin torculāre, from Latin torculum.
From Vulgar Latin *tōnsāre, frequentative of Latin tondeō, through its past participle, tōnsus. Compare Portuguese tosar.

parole.significato: to leave (a mark, impression, or imprint); to trace
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tractiāre, from Latin tractus.

Potentially from Vulgar Latin *trānsfrīcō (“to rub across”), from trans- + frico; Klein instead suggests the Italian has ultimate origin in Arabic تَفْرِيق (tafrīq, “distribution, dispersion”), reshaped to match the native prefix tra- (“trans-”). Cognate with Piedmontese tràfich/tràfic and Sicilian
From Vulgar Latin *trilicius < Latin trilicem.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *traxīnāre, from *tragīnāre from *tragere, from Classical Latin trahere. Compare French traîner, Spanish trajinar. Cf. also the doublet trainare.
From Vulgar Latin *tribla, from syncopation of Latin tribŭla.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *triblāre, from Latin tribulāre. Doublet of the borrowed tribolare.
From Vulgar Latin *triccāre, present infinitive of *triccō, from Late Latin trīcāre, from Latin trīcārī (“to behave evasively; to play tricks”), derived from trīcae (“trumpery”).
From Vulgar Latin trecentum, from Latin trecenti.

Via a dialect or language from Northern Italy, from Vulgar Latin *trānsienda (“which is to be passed”), from Latin trānseō (“to traverse, go over, pass over”). Cf. also dialectal tresenda, tresanda (“lane”).
From Vulgar Latin *tremāre, from Classical Latin tremere.
From Vulgar Latin *trena, from Latin trina (“triple”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin trīstus, from Latin trīstis. Doublet of triste, a borrowing from Latin.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *terebella, diminutive of Latin terebra (“gimlet”).
From Vulgar Latin *tropāre, a verb probably based on Classical Latin tropus. Compare French trouver.
From Vulgar Latin *tūrāre, from Latin obtūrāre. Compare the doublet otturare.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin tōttus, alteration of Latin tōtus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *hōque annō, alteration of Latin hōc annō.
From Vulgar Latin *ungla, syncopated form of Latin ungula, from unguis.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin (*)ŏvum, from Latin ōvum n.
With rebracketing, from earlier lusignolo, lusignuolo, from Vulgar Latin *lusciniolus, derived from Latin luscinia. Compare rosignolo.
From Vulgar Latin *valliāre, from Latin vallus, from Proto-Indo-European *wal- (“stick, stake”).
From vagliare, from Vulgar Latin *valliāre, from Latin vallus, from Proto-Indo-European *wal- (“stick, stake”).

parole.significato: a small valley between steep faces
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *valleus, derived from Classical Latin vallis (“valley”).
From Vulgar Latin *variō, variōnem, from Latin varius (“variegated”).
From Vulgar Latin or Late Latin vānitāre, from Latin vānus or vānitās. Compare French vanter.
From Vulgar Latin missōrium, crossed with Latin vās.
From Latin viduus, through a Vulgar Latin *viduvus.
From Vulgar Latin *vēla, from the plural of Latin vēlum. Doublet of voile.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ventrisca, derived from Classical Latin venter (“belly”).
From Vulgar Latin *ventriclu, from syncopation of Latin ventriculus. Doublet of ventricolo and ventriglio.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *viridizāre. Derivable from verde (“green”) + -eggiare (verb-forming suffix).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin vēredictum, from Latin vēre + dictum.
From verde + -ezza or Vulgar Latin *viriditia.
From verde (“green”) + -ura (“noun-forming suffix”), or from Vulgar Latin *virdūra.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *verecunnia, from Latin verēcundia, possibly influenced by cunnus (“vagina”). Doublet of verecondia, which was borrowed. Compare Galician vergoña ~ vergonza, but Portuguese and Occitan vergonha, Sicilian virigogna ~ vrigogna, Spanish vergüenza.

parole.significato: any of several varieties of white grape cultivated in Liguria, Tuscany and Sardinia
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *hībernācea.
From Vulgar Latin *verruculum, alteration of Latin vericulum (“small rod”).
From Vulgar Latin *virdia (“cabbage”), from Late Latin virdis (“green”) (via the neuter plural), syncopated from Classical Latin viridis.
From Vulgar Latin *vicāta, from Latin vicis. Doublet of fiata, which was borrowed from Old French.
From Vulgar Latin *volūculum, derived from Latin volvō (“to roll, wrap”). Possibly a cognate of viluppo.
From a Vulgar Latin root *vinctus, itself an alteration of Latin victus, or contracted from a form *vincitus as a variant participle of vincō.
From Vulgar Latin *visclum, contraction of *visculum, from Latin viscum.
From Vulgar Latin *vītignus, thought to have a separate origin from Latin vītigenus (“produced by the vine”) and Late Latin vītineus (“of or pertaining to the vine”).
From Vulgar Latin *vīvanda, from Latin vīvenda, from the neuter plural form of vīvendus, from vīvere (“to live”), or more likely borrowed from French viande
Possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *vetius, from Latin vetus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin volēre, regularized from Latin velle.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vol(vi)tāre, derived from Latin volvere.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin root *voltus < *volvitus or *volŭtus, from Latin volūtus, perfect passive participle of volvō. Cognate with Sicilian votu~vutatu.

parole.significato: to roll (a boulder, a barrel, etc.)
parole.testo: Probably from a Vulgar Latin *volutulāre, from Classical Latin volūtus, past participle of volvō.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *volūtum, past participle for volēre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin vōscum, from Latin vōbīscum.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vocitum.

parole.significato: to have a limp, to walk with a limp
parole.testo: From zoppo + -icare, or inherited from Vulgar Latin *cloppicāre, from Late Latin cloppus. Compare Sicilian zuppijari.

From Vulgar Latin, Late Latin cloppus, perhaps ultimately imitative of a limping person. The Italian was possibly altered by influence from zanca. Compare Romanian șchiop, cf. also Catalan and Occitan esclop, Old French clop and Sicilian zoppu.

From Vulgar Latin *sūfilāre, from Latin sībilāre, whence also the doublets sibilare and sobillare. Cognate with Corsican zifulà, Venetan sifołar, Romansh tschüvler, tschivlar, Norman sûfflier, Walloon xhufler (Old French sufler).
Probably a dialectal variant of girlo crossed with Vulgar Latin *currūlus, diminutive of currus (“chariot; plough rollers”).
From a- + lungo + -are or from a Vulgar Latin root *allongāre, from ad + Late Latin longāre (cf. also elongāre), from Latin longus. Compare French allonger.
Probably from Vulgar Latin *alima, dissimilated form of Latin anima (compare Spanish and Portuguese alma); alternatively, a borrowing from Old Occitan (compare Occitan anma, arma). Doublet of anima.
From amaro + -ezza, or from a Vulgar Latin *amāritia, from Latin amāritiēs.

parole.significato: to drizzle, to wet slightly (as if with dew)
parole.testo: Either inherited or borrowed from Old Occitan arozar or Old French arroser; in all cases from Vulgar Latin *arrosāre, itself from Latin adrorō. First attested before 1250.

parole.significato: to equip, to fit out, to tool up
parole.testo: Uncertain. Possibly from attrezzo, itself possibly from French attraits. Alternatively from Vulgar Latin *attrectiāre, from Latin attrectāre.
From balza or possibly a Vulgar Latin root *balteanus, from Latin balteus. Compare also Old French bauçant.
Possibly inherited from Vulgar Latin *bastōnem, itself a modification of Late Latin bastum, or possibly noun use of the verb *bastō, from Ancient Greek βαστάζω (bastázō). Compare French bâton.

Inherited from Old Italian biastema, from Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin blasphēmia (remodeled after the verb bestemmiare, or alternatively through a Vulgar Latin form *blastemia), from Ancient Greek βλασφημία (blasphēmía).
Probably from Old French bouton, from the verb bouter, or alternatively possibly from Vulgar Latin *bottonem or *botonus.

From Vulgar Latin *bottia, a Germanic borrowing, from Frankish *boce (“knob”), from Old High German bozzan (“to beat”), from Proto-West Germanic *bautan (“to push, strike”). The origin is uncertain. Could be from Catalan brisa, influenced by rezze. Alternatively, from Vulgar Latin *brevidia, derived from a word which gave rise to Italian breva.
From Vulgar Latin *brocca, from either Ancient Greek πρόχοος (prókhoos, “vessel for water”), or from βροχίς (brokhís, “inkwell”), with influence from broccus. Further a cognate to Albanian prokë.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *burius (“red, dark”), either from Latin burrus (“reddish-brown”) or, less likely, from Latin furvus (“dark, dusky”).

From caldo or from a Vulgar Latin root *caldūra, from Latin caldus, calidus. Compare Romanian căldură.

Deverbal from cambiare + -o. From verb cambiare inherited from Vulgar Latin cambiāre (“to change, exchange”) from Late Latin cambiō, or from corresponding noun Latin cambium (“change”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂emp- (“to bend, curve”). Compare Spanish cambio and Portuguese câmbio.

parole.significato: to hoop (put hoops around a barrel, etc.)
parole.testo: From cerchio + -are, or alternatively from a Vulgar Latin *circlāre < Late Latin circulāre, from Latin circulārī, and therefore doublet of the borrowing circolare. Compare French cercler.
From Vulgar Latin or Late Latin īsicia, plural of īsicium (“minced meat”), from īnsicium < Latin īnsecō (“cut up”). Compare Spanish chicha. Alternatively, from a syncope of carniccia.

From a Vulgar Latin derivative of Latin ieiūnium. The initial Latin ie- or je- may have changed to de- over time, leading to di- in Italian. Compare the similar Catalan dejuni. Alternatively digiuno may have been regressively derived from the verb digiunare, and was independent of this Latin word.

parole.significato: to issue, to put out, to release, to disseminate (an invitation, press release, etc.)
parole.testo: From di- + ramo, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *dērāmāre, from Latin rāmus (“branch”). Compare Romanian dărâma, Dalmatian dramur, Old French deramer, Spanish and Portuguese derramar; compare also Albanian dërmoj.

Probably a back-formation of doccione (“conduit, spout”), from Latin ductiōnem, from ducere, infinitive of dūcō (“lead, guide; draw, pull”), or alternatively from a Vulgar Latin root *ducea, ultimately from the same root. Compare Dozza, a borrowing from Emilian Dòza.
From doglia + -oso or from a Vulgar Latin root *doliōsus, from Latin dolor. Compare Romanian duios, Friulian duliôs.

Contraction/syncopation of diritto, from Vulgar Latin *dērēctus (or from Late Latin drictus; compare French droit, Catalan dret, Romanian drept, Sicilian drittu), from Latin dīrēctus. Doublet of diretto.

parole.significato: to fail to germinate (of a seed)
parole.testo: From fallo + -are or falla + -are, from Vulgar Latin *falla, or from Late Latin fallāre, from Latin fallere.
Borrowed from Occitan fermalh or from French fermail, in either case from Vulgar Latin *firmāc(u)lum, derived from Latin firmāre (“make fast”).
Inherited from Latin fābula (> ˈfabla > 'fabbja > ˈfjabᵇa), or alternatively through a Vulgar Latin form *flaba from metathesis of *fabla. Doublet of favola and fola.

From forno + -ello (“diminutive suffix”), or from Vulgar Latin *furnellus, from Latin furnus. Compare French fourneau, Sicilian furneddu, Catalan fornell, Romansh furnel, Sardinian furredhu, Occitan fornèl, Portuguese fornilho, Spanish hornillo.

parole.significato: to shred, to rip into pieces
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French frapper, fraper, or from Vulgar Latin frappāre; both from Frankish *hrapōn (“to jerk; snatch”).
From fritto + -ura, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *frīctūra, from Latin frīctus. Compare French friture, Romanian friptură, Spanish and Portuguese fritura, Sicilian frittura.
From gocciare or from a Vulgar Latin *guttia or *guttea; ultimately from Latin gutta.

From gargozza, or gargozzo, itself from an onomatopoeic root garg- or from Vulgar Latin *gurgutia or *gargutium. Probably from grovigliolo, from an alteration of rubiglio. Or possibly connected with Latin globus via a Vulgar Latin *globilia.
Possibly from a Vulgar Latin gruma, from Latin grumus, or alternatively of Germanic origin.
From im (“in”) + bocca (“mouth”) + -are, or from a Vulgar Latin *imbuccāre, from Latin bucca. Compare Spanish and Catalan embocar, French emboucher, Romanian îmbuca.

parole.significato: to turn green, to green, to make green
parole.testo: Either from in- + verde + -ire, or from a Vulgar Latin *invir(i)dire, from *invir(i)descere, from Latin viridēscere. Compare Romanian înverzi, Catalan enverdir, Spanish enverdir, enverdecer, Portuguese enverdecer, French verdir.
From lavare + -tura, or from a Vulgar Latin *lavatūra, from Latin lavō. Compare French lavure, Sicilian lavatura, Spanish lavadura, Romanian lături.

From a Vulgar Latin *liccāre (compare French lécher), itself probably from Proto-West Germanic *likkōn. See English lick for more. Borrowed from Old French madrier or from Old Occitan madier, ultimately from Vulgar Latin *māterium, from Latin māteria (“matter; timber”).

parole.significato: to be lacking, to be missing (of objects)
parole.testo: From manco (adjective) + -are, or from a Vulgar Latin *mancāre, from Latin mancus.
From minuzzare, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *minūtiālia, from Latin minūtia. Compare Friulian minuçae, Old French menuisaille, Portuguese miuçalha, Aromanian minutsalji.
From minuzza /minuzzare + -ame or from a Vulgar Latin *minūtiamen, from Latin minūtia.

From Latin mūtulus, syncopated to *mutlus, or from cumulus, transposed to a Vulgar Latin form *muculus > *muclus. Based on the first etymology, mutulo is a doublet, and based on the second, cumulo and cumolo are.

Uncertain; either from Vulgar Latin *nīdiculāre (“to stay in one's nest”), from Latin nīdus (“nest”), or from Vulgar Latin *hinnitulāre, from Latin hinniō (“to neigh, whinny”), possibly even from a merger of the two.
From oliva or from Vulgar Latin olīvus, from Latin olīva, olīvum.
Feminine of palombo or from Vulgar Latin palumba, from Latin palumbus.

Probably from Vulgar Latin *pedinus, a derivative of Latin pedem (“foot”). Compare Sicilian pèdinu, Romanian piedin, Albanian pedim. Alternatively from Latin pendulus. Less likely linked to penna / pinna (“feather”).
From penzolo + -are or from Vulgar Latin *pendiolāre, from *pendiolus, from Latin pendulus, from pendō.

From pugno, or from a Vulgar Latin *pūgnālis, from Latin pugnus. Compare Spanish puñal, Portuguese punhal, Catalan punyal, French poignard (Old French poignal).

parole.significato: to twist again, to retwist (wire, etc.)
parole.testo: From ri- + torcere (“to twist”), or from Vulgar Latin *retorcere, from Latin retorquēre.
